The awe and wonder which its employment first excited have long ago given place to a settled conviction that it represents a power which man has at his disposal, and which can be made to do all sorts of hitherto impossible tasks. The electric battery, for most purposes where an electric current is required, is giving place to the economical dynamo-machine,' in which magnets form the source whence the electricity is drawn. The old frictional machine is seldom seen outside the lec- ture theatre, where it is still used to instructsthe young in the principles of electric science. What is known as fric- tional electricity has not often been applied to any useful purpose, save that of education. Recently, however, a clever adaptation of it has been conceived by Mr. Kingsland Smith—a transatlantic miller—in the construction of a puri- fier of flour, which separates the bran and middlings from the finer material. The flour, shaken mechanically, so as to bring the coarser particles to the surface, is passed beneath an indiarubber-covered cylinder, which revolves against a fixed rubber. The effect is the same as that which occurs on rubbing a piece of sealing-wax ; the cylinder is elec- trified, and the particles of bran are attracted to it, until they are scraped off into a receptacle prepared for them. The finer flour then passes away, quite-freed from its im- purities. The proprietor of the mill where this electric purifier has been in constant use for acme time estimates that the saving effectea by it amounts to 10 cents, per barrel of -flour. We may mention that the separation was formerly effected 'by Air-blasts, necessitating extra engine- povser, as well as costln wear and tear.—Chambers's Journal. Eraserare TRAMWAYS AND VELOCIPEDES.—The electric tramway which Dr. Wei-rim:Siemens has constructed in Ber- lin between the suburb of Lichtenfeld and the Cadettenhaus is now regularly opened for passengers, and is giving great satisfaction. The rails are of the ordinary railway pattern, but the gauge is only 3fl. 3in. A single car is propelled by the current at an average speed of nine miles an hour, though this rate can be doubled if necessary. A similar line has been erected at the Crystal Palace, Sydenham, as an at- traction for visitors, but it is probable that electric tramways will be practically introduced into this country before many years are past. Velocipedes are now so common that it is not surprising to find that electrieity has been applied to their propulsion. M. Trouve, the well-known French elec- trician, recently drove an English tricycle through the streets of Paris by means of electricity stored in a Plante secondary battery and a pair of Deprez electric motors. The tricycle, with its occupant and apparatus, veighed 4 cwt., and went at the speed of an ordinary cab; but with some modification of the apparatus M. Trouve hopes to attain a rate of 12 or 15 miles an hour. The new secondary battery of M. Faure will also help his purpose, and we may antici- pate that velocipedes driven by eleetric power will by-and- by prove useful to the invalided or the weakly. This earthly chaos, with its vaporous air, Cannot all things with clouds 36 dense o'erlay, But that the glowing sun's refulgent ray Can the dark mantle penetrate and tear. Scornful ingratitude, manner severe, Are the obstructing cloud, that can but sway, -14 While Heaven forbears to drive vain hopes away, .Attd change its favours into dark despair; • The rolling earth can Heaven in night obscure, The sun may e'en for bears eclipsed remain, But cannot be for ever overlaid; 14 And so thy warfare may awhile endure, • But V and by,. in Spite of clouds and rain, Thy, Sun will be declared and be obeyed. —Seventy Smmets of Camoens: By J. TILE STORK'S JEREMIAD. "One-legged stork, thou standest sad and lonely; A tear, methinks, I notice in thine eyes; Oh, tell to me, yes, whisper to me only, What is the sorrow which I think I spy ?" And 10, from out the meshes of the tidy - There came a feeble, mournful sort of squeak; " And while, amazed, I opened my eyes wide, he Opened his mouth, and thus began to speak "I am so very tired of being artistic; My life is one long, patient, painful ache ; I am so weary of these weird and mystic Positions which they force my form to take. "They've worked me in all kinds and sorts of stitches. High art and button-hole, outline and cross stitch, Standing around promiscuously in ditches, And looking like a buzzard or an ostrich. " They've worked me frequently on Java canvas, On momie-cfloth, on flannels thin and thick; In fact. in every single way they can fuss, I have appeared, until I'm really sick. " In crewels, in silk, in worsted, and in cotton, Now black, now white, now grave, now madly gay, They've worked me, and one wrong is unforgotten, they've done me most and worst in applique. " Sometimes they plant me 'mid some rushes speary, In attitudes no well-bred stork would take, Holding one leg up, tin I get so weary I sometimes think my poor strained back will break. "They've worked me standing, running, sleeping, flying; Sometimes I'm gazing at a crewel sun; They've worked me every way, I think, but dying; And oh, I wish they'd do that, and be done I "I could forgive them all this bitter wronging, If they would grant one favour, which I beg, Would gratify but once my soul's deep longing, Just to put down my cramped and unused leg. "Know you of any one with sorrows greater? A. creature with a life that's more forlorn? Hounded for ever by the Decorator; I wish, I wish, I never had been born I" Aeilence fell. I gazed; he had subsided ; -1 listened vainly. All was dumb and still Upon the tidy, where the stork resided, Witlimheld leg, and red and open bill. '2lvasztry.

PARTIAL PLANTS.—The rocky clefts of the Steep Holme are still crimson in May and June with the brilliant red blossoms of the wild pony, a flower which does not else- where appear nearer to England than the Pyrenees. Some months since, when I had the pleasure of personally con- ducting the readers of the Cornhill on a philological tour through the Lyme Regis district, we stopped for a few minutes at the pretty little village of Kilmington, near Ax- minster. Well, Kilmington Common is a place famous to botanists, because it is the one single station in Britain for a small purplish lobelia, which ranges elsewhere only from Andalusia to central France. Dozens of like cases may be noticed in the south-western peninsula of England, and the similarly situatod corner of Wales about Pembrokeshire. Thus, to lump a long list briefly, the common blue monks- hood is found wild in South Wales and the Cornish District only; the yellow drabs is confined to old walls about Pen- nerd Castle, near Swansea ; the spotted rock-cistue occurs only in the Channel Islands and at Holyhead; the white rock-cistus is peculiar in Britain to Brent Downs in Somer- set, together with Torquay and Babbicombe in Devon; the Cheddar pink, a volcanic plant of southern Europe, clings to the crannies of the Cheddar cliffs near Wells, and to no other crag in England; the soapwort is wild only in Corn- wall and Devon; the flax-leaved St. John's wort grows no- where but at Cape Cornwall and on the banks of the Tejo; the crimson clover and Boccone's clover are entirely re- stricted to the peninsula of the Lizard ; so also is the up- right clover, save that it is likewise found in the Channel Islands; the sand bird's foot remains only at Scilly; the Bithynian vetch extends through Europe as far north as Bourdeaux, and then disappears again till after a sudden leap it is gathered ones more in Devon and Cornwall; .the white sedum occurs in the Malvern hills and in Somerset- shire; and the narrow buplever flowers only at Torquay and in Jersey and Guernsey. In almost all, if not in all, these cases, the plant is a southern one, which extends usually from the Caspian to Spain, is perhaps found as far north as the Gironde or even the Loire, and then disappears again till it turns up suddenly in some exceptionally shel- tered nook of Devon, Cornwall, or South Wales. This is a ' phenomenon which cannot surely be due to chance alone. Indeed, I might greatly increase the list, but I refrain only ; because lam afraid of being wearisome. When we turn to the similarly placed south-western corner of Ireland, the peculiarities we meet with are even more remarkable. I' shall never forget my surprise when once, after my first Visit to Nice and Mentone, I began describing the beautiful I Provencal flowers to an Irish botanist, and was quietly answered, "Ah, yes; we have them all at Killarney.' But it is really true none the less. The thick-leaved sedum, after skipping all England and Wales, shows itself suddenly in the Cove of Cork. The pretty Mediterranean heath, which every winterer on the Riviera has gathered by hand- fuls on the hills about Cannes and Hveres, jumps at a bound to the coast of Kerry. The arbutus, with its clus- tering white blossoms and beautiful red berries, is similarly found in Provence and again at Glengariff. London pride grows wild in Portugal, western Spain, and the higher Pyrenees, and re•appears in south-western Ireland. Another pretty little saxifrage jumps in like manner from the As- turias to Killarney. St. Dabeoc's heath has the same range. The spiked orchid takes a great bound from Bordeaux to a single station in County Galway. To sum it up shortly, 'Crete, Auvergne, the Pyrenees, S.-W. Ireland," is a com- mon technical description ot .the distribution of many south European plants.—Cornhill Magazine.

WRAC Is LITERATIME P—Books have been written on every subject in which men are interested. The architect, the engineer, the lawyer, the doctor consult books that will help them in their professions; but law books, and medical books, and books on architecture—books written fora special class—are not literature. On the other hand, books written in verse or prose that awaken thought, that give solaCe and delight, and lift us above the narrow round of our daily lives—books that make us happier, wiser, even merrier—are books that deserve to be called literature. Our poets, our historians, our essayists, our novelists, the travellers who describe what they have seen in different parts of the world, the critics who write about books and show us their faults and beauties, have all contributed to build up what we call our national literature, by which we mean the literature produced by Englishmen. Every great people has produced a noble literature, and this is indeed, one of the chief signs of its greatness. We read the literature of the Jews in the books which form our Bible; ancient Greece produced a literature unequalled in Europe to this day for beauty of language and wealth of thought; Rome, that once ruled the world, did so first by the sword, then by her laws, and then by the poets and historians that:have made the Latin lan- guage so famous. Modern nations, too—such as Germany, France, and Italy—can each boast a national literature ; but not one of these countries has a literature equal to that which is open to readers of the English language.—Good Words.

• LANCASIIIRE AND 'FREE TRADE. • The letter which we give below, and the terse note which follows it, are from the Agricultural Gazette. "True Briton " is falling into an error that may mislead many. His facts are wrong, for England is far from falling into bankruptcy, as the decrease in her National Debt and the increase in her savings show. Several succeeding bad sea- sons have pressed very hardly on the farming clase, but it would have profited them little to have decreatied the pur- chasing power of the manufacturing classes by taxing them to subsidise farmers. "Protectionist nations are prospering wonderfully "is not more true than the supposed decline of Britain, or else why the stream of emigrants from Germany, which has just increased its tuffs ? Security for the farmers' capital. by improved Land Laws would do more to improve their position than depriving foreign nations of the power to buy from us, by refusing to take what they send us in exchange. "The late election at Preston gives cheering *Videlicet that many Lancashire people have bad enowth of dnó-sided Free Trade. Now, as the Free Trade Act was passed in obedience to the demands of the manufacturing towns, en- forced as those demands were by bread riots and so forth, it is fitting and proper that the same towns should now con- fess that Free. Trade had not come up to their expectations, and should demand a reversal of that policy. I wish to speak with all respect of the late Mr. Cobden and Mr. Bright. Their honesty and sincerity were unquestionable; they thought that England must always be the workshop of the world; that competition with her in manufactures, ma- chinery, or mining must always be hopeless, a dream to smile at, and circumstances helped to foster this pleasing de- lusion for a considerable time. Daring these years we often heard that our prosperity resulted from Free Trade, and that the nations of the world, seeing our wealth accumulat- ing, were sure to follow our example lit abolishing their tariffe on imports. Now the late Mr. Hermon—a candid and , wise man—said, with much justice, that our commercial prosperity up to 1870 had very little to do either with Free Trade or Protection. He thought the discoveries of gold, facilities for locomotion, and transit of goods had far more to do with it. Perhaps I may be allowed- to mention a factor which,. in my humble opinion, had more to do with our increase of wealth than any other cause : I refer to the fact that for many years we were practically unopposed in manufacturing, &c.; and this because our great rivals, France and the United States, were engaged in exhausting wars, which lamed and weakened both of them for years. We see also that since our Crimean war all the great Powers of Europe have been successively engaged in that costly game, as well as many secondary Powers. When countries are struggling for existence, they are far more concerned about the manufacture of war material than of textile fabrics; hence our commercial prosperity in those years. But since 1871 competition has begun with a vengeance. All the predictions of the Cobden school have been falsified. Protectionist nations are prosperity wonderfully, while the only free-trading nation is sinking into poverty, if not abso- lute insolvency, and all for an idea. Now I can easily ex- cuse Mr. Bright for still upholding his favourite doctrines; and I can understand that no amount of evideo,ce will ever convince him that English attempts to convert the world to Free Trade principles have proved a disastrous failure---the man has risen to great eminence by steadfastly declaring that it is everyone's interest to buy in the cheapest market, whether the seller may be friend or foe; we really have no right to expect him to take an unbiassed view of the ques- tion. Mr. Bright informs the electors of Preston that "there is no man whose political views are more generally wrong than Mr. Ecroyd's ;" the answer they make to this manifesto is to elect Mr. Ecroyd by a tremendous majority, in a battle fought simply between a Protectionist and a Free Trader. Lancashire thinks and acts to-day, the rest of Eng- land "to-morrow or after." "ant then we must not put tax on food, the country would not stand that," cry some ; why not? The country stands a heavy tax on beer, which maqy people consider a part oe their food; but Mr. Her- mon's proposal to give a bounty of so much per acre on all grain crops grown in the kingdom will do equally well: that plan would arrest the downward course of agriculture time,hmoe aantlttbeheraym sign gn offered at a merely and prevent much land-going out of cultivation—and no one can say: but there are numerous farms not 60 masa from Lon* ,niedtsoumeenotof lt3l;:etmoofporronoudretont liesstsohnat a good "r neighbours. The House met at four o'clock. ViratLatio LB/Gum—Mr. D. ONSLOW asked whether the toverntnent intended to retain in the service of the Crown officials holding office under the Land League.—Mr. GLAD,. STONE said he did not believe that persons strictly within that designation were members of the Lar,d League. The only cases of the kind in which it would, Ise possible to apply that designation were that of a Roman Catholic priest who received an allowance for occasional duty and of a collector of income tax. They were not able to say that according to the law the Land League, was an illegal asso- ciation.

div.head: CO-OPERATIVE MOVEMENT.
div.p: THE CO-OPERATIVE MOVEMENT.

Public meetings were held on Saturday, at Leedd;Wakee field, Dewsbury, Keighley, Heckmondwike, SowiThy Bridge and other places, in connection with the thirteenth annual co-operative congress. Mr. Barran, M.P., who presided at the Leeds meeting, referred to the early struggles and the etrong prejudice which the pioneers of the -co-operative movement had to contend against. These difficulties had now been overcome, and co-operation was now recognised as a power in the land. Of its usefulness there was no donbt, as through it many families had been able to .obtain neces- saries they were before deprived of. Lord Derby presided on Monday at the opening of the operative Congress at Leeds, and delivered the inaugural ad- dress. He said that voluntary associations on a large scale, asking no help from the State but only freedom and non-in- terference, were a marked and peculiar characteristic of our age; and it was to his mind not the least of the merits of the co-operative movement that was kept strictly within the limits of that principle. It did not clamour for public money; it did not ask that its opponents should be put down by the strong arm of the law; nor did it over-ride free contract or meddle with individual liberties. The noble Lord discussed the main features of co-operation, and ob- served that 44 of all the ten thousand schemes hitherto pro. posed—and there is a new one about every six weeks—for closing the long-standing differences between the labottr and capital, co-operation is that which promisee thelargest re- sults with the fewest drawbacks." Taking-stock of the present situation, he presumed they might lay .clown that co-operation for productive purposes, though doing well and flourishing was, on the whole, still in the expetimental stage, and that co-operation in agricultural matters was still practically untried. He certainly should hesitate to advise anyoneto take to farming just ngw who looked for large re- turnt.: Yet there was something to be said on the other side; land was cheaper to rent or to buy than it had been for twenty years past. If they could find men of the rightsort. —men accustomed to agricultural work, willing to put them- selves under orders, though they were their ovrn- masters, and.intelligent enough not to be disheartened and throw up the game if they were not lucky at the outset—the empire- relent would probably answer. If they could not find such men it had better tot be tried. The business of the Con- ference embraced the discussion of various subjects, 'chiefly the investment of the surplus funds.of co-operative societies.

"Gtass HousEs."—Mr. Henry Richard, has written, in the Herald of Peace, an ablsreply to an - Austrian military alarmist, and pessimist, whomn a grand- motherly style has, in an influential periodical, endeavoured to frighten Englishmen bra melancholy picture of their insufficient armaments, from an Austrian pointof view. Ent Mr. Richard shows that "those who live in glass-houses must not throw stones," and easily proves that Austria has long resided in a very fragile " glass-house ; " as her own arma- ments did not prevent her being thoroughly smashed up by the Germans in the Seven Days War of 1866. Nor did her "pipe clay " perfection of militarism enable her to with- stand riance at Magenta. And 'still, to-day, Austria is a deceptive" Power "—blown out, but weak and hollow, and deeply involved in debt. Mr. Richard remarks When a man volunteers an indictment against his neighbour, and charges with sitter incapacity his management of his domestic ,affairs, it is..not unnatural to ask how such an officious accneer manages his own. If Austria is to teach England how to live, surely we may, without impertinence, inquire how Austria herself is living. We may take for granted that this gallant officer, before presuming to lecture Great Britain on her military impotence, has satisfied himself that his own country is in a satisfactory condition. Certainly no one can Charge Austria with hexing neglected the military element in nationallife. And with what results? With this result, ,4" ene thing—that since 1789 there has not been a single • Year in whieh her revenue has come up to expenditure. The accumulated deficits of Austria from 1851 to 1866 amounted to £130,000,000. And it is still going on. According to Mr. Martin's " Statesman's Year Book," tin; deficits between 1870 land 1877 have amounted to £17,000,000. Another result which Austria has gained from her military life is this that r her debt has grown from £12500,000 in 1848 to £391,000,000 lin 1880. Robert Davies and Co.) , appeared for the defence.—P. S. Spinks said on Thursday the 2nd, June, about half-past seven, he was going along Lythgoes-lane in company with P. C. Manner, when he saw the defendant Multcarn standing about- three feet from; the defendant's house with a blue jug in his hand, and from whith he was drinking. Happening to turn his head, 'Multcarn saw the officers and immediately hastened into Furness' provision shop. The officers entered the beer- house, and asked the girl in charge, who appeared to he about 13 years of age, where the jug was Multcara had drank from. The girl replied, "He got the jug from the other shop which has nothing to do with this." Witness then went across the road to the provision shop, which Was in charge of Furness' son,. who after much hesitation handed witness the jug, stating. that he had sold it to a man who had just gone out, but he ate, vards retracted that statement. The jug had contained beer.—P.C. Chantler corroborated.—Mr. Slater, for the de- feree, said the sth and 6th sections of the Licensing Act 1872, were passed not to enforce the practice of a few for malities, but to stop people from taking advantages of pre.. ceding Acts, to erect small wooden hats outside ,the 'beer- house but near to the door, to which beer could be carried. He quoted a similar case to, the present one, in which it had been held that no offence had been committed, and contended' that no convictions could be ,te3orded against the defendant unless the act had been ,done by his consent; and he was prepared to prove lit it was done without his knowledge er consent.—Alice Furness, defendant's daughter, said she remembered Mult- carn-going into the beer house and asking for a pint of beer, bathe had no jug, and she told him they could not allow it to be drunk in the house. He went out but shortly after- Wards returned with a jug, and she supplied him with the beerio Shedid not know where he got the jug, nor where he drank the beer. She had told P.S. Spinks she did not know where Maltearn got the jug.—A girl eight years of age was called i but not sworn, who stated she lent the jug to the defendant,but did not know what it was for.—The Chairman said the Bench did not think the case proved, and it would therefore be dismissed.

'CIIARGE OF OBTAINING GOODS DY FALSE PRETENCES.— George William Bogwick, alias George Padwick, was charged with obtaining 10 tons of manure by false pretences from W. H. King, manure manufacturer, Liverpool, through his agent, Isaac Brundrit, of Sale.—Mr. Rice (Messrs. iluckton and Greenall) appeared for the complainant, and Mr. Moore for the defendant —Mr. Rice said that on the 20th April Mr. Brundrit attended the Warrington market, where he met the defendant, who told hush, wanted to Purchase a quantity of manure. Defendant stated he occu- pied a farm under Sir Richard Brooke, but Was about to quit and take another at Sutton Weaver. He ordered 10 tons of manure, and in consequence of defendant's representations the order was executed. He gave his name as Geo. Padwick, and told Mr. Brundrit to address his letters to Halton post-office. It bad since been discovered that de- fendant was a farm labourer.—Mr. Brundrit said if he liad known defendant was a farm labourer he would not have accepted the order. Defendant promised to pay for the manure on the following Wednesday. On that day he ad- mitted having received the manure, but stated that he bad beta young horse, and could not then pay for it.—Cross- examined : No pgrson was present when the order was given. He had heard that defeadant had some land at that time. Defendant offered to pay witness £5 on account. Defendant had stated that he was prepared to keep to the bargain if he had the usual six months' credit. Defendant me his name as Padwick, and he had never told him that his name was Bodwick.—Robert Holland, agent to Sir ltd. Brooke, said he knew the defendant by the name of Wm. Padwick, but the name was so unfamiliar that it was pro- nounced in several different ways, and he was also known as Bodwick. He lived in a cotttage on Sir Richard's estate and was a labourer. Ile also dealt in cattle to some extent and undertook, sometimes, large contracts in the way of cleaning out ditches, lze. By Mr. White: Last year he occupied four acres of land and cultivated it himself. lie occupLd the land on the 20th April but was not now,in possession. Mr. Moore submitted that there was no cTse against his client and be was surprised that Messrs. King should bring such a case into the police court. The Bench held that no case had been made out and the summons was therefore dismissed, complainant being ordered to pay defen- dant his advocate's fee of 10s. 6d. THE EXTRAORDINARY CASE OF ASSAULT.—John Mannion, a young man, was charged with assaulting Jane Hennessy, on Monday. The case had been adjourned from Wednesday, in order that a man, stated to have really committed the assault, might be apprehended, but his apprehension had not been effected. There being no evidence to prove that defendant bad struck the women, he was discharged. Tun CHARGE OF UNLAWFUL WOUNDING. Mary Gil- garry was charged with assaulting Ellen McCormick, on Monday last. The case had been adjourned from Tuesday last as complainant could not appear in consequence of her injuries. She now stated she did not wish to press the case as defendant was a "woman with a big family, and had been a good neighbour to her."—Defendant admitted striking the complainant, and the Bench considered the case one which they could not overlook, and defendant was bound over to , keep the peace for six mouths.

during 64 :14.years of their existence had scarcely been of that subedikial nature that with an organisation such as their own they might reasonably expect, and there was manta to believe Vie establishment expenses would be little We number of are-than they were now if they had double th members. In 1845 1. comprised 13000—members, who seceded from the Manchester Unity. Prom 1845 to 1861 the number increased to 23,568, from 1861 to 1866 the increase had been to 29,654, from 18i to 1871 the in- crease was to 35,645, from 1871 to 1876 it was increased to 41,200, and dur:ng the four years ending 1180,the in- crease was 49,916. During the year 1877 and 1878 they made no progress, and very little in 1879, a fact attributable to the long period of depression and stagnation in trade; but 1830 had been the best recorded in the annals of the society, and had made amends for the three previous years, when they found it difficult to hold their own for the increase in the past year had been upwards of 4,000 members. The prosperity of the past year had not been colfined to mem- bers only, as their funds had increased from £123,746 14s sid to £128,423 4s lid. He hoped the time was not far distant when every district and lodge in the Order would! become registered.

THE FREE GARDENERS. The business of the annual general meeting of the dele- gates of the National United Order of Free Gardeners' Friendly Society was commenced at the Church Tnstitate, Leeds, on Monday. Mr. George Turner, the Grand Master of the Order, presided, there being present about 100 dele- gates from various parts of the country.—The President, in opening the proceedings, said that notwithstanding ce - tions Of many lodges during the year, the Executive Corn- mittee was able to report a large increase both in number of members and in funds. While last year they had to declare a decrease of 6,295, they had this year initiated 5,897 members, which, deducting for suspended, expelled, and deaths 3,906, and for cessations 386, left a total increase of 1,102 members for the year. (Hear, hear.) There were 441 honorary members, 665 lodges, and 82 districts. Whilst last year the funds showed a total gain of £3,680 13s sd, they this year showed A gain of £6,142 13s 3d. There had been paid for sick and funerals during the year £32,314 Os so, and for manageinent £8,134 17s 41a, making a total forsick, funerals, and management of £40,448 17s Bd. The returns, as far as they had been received; showed the *work of the lodges and districts to be, on the 31st Deceit:abet last, as fol- lows: Lodge funds £75,141 5s 30, and district: funds, £17,345 18s 100, making a total of £92,487 4s 2d, and if they took into consideration the lodges and districts which had failed to send in returns the worth of the Order would be more than £lOO,OOO. (Applause.)—A dem:dation, con- sisting of representatives of the Ancient Order of Foresters, the Ashton Unity of Shepherds, the Ancient Order of' Romans, and the British Unity of Oddlellows, attended the meeting, aisd welcomed the delegates to the town. ' THE GRANIPITNITED ORDER OF ODDFELLOWS. , . On Monday the biennial meeting of delegates_ of this, Order opened in the Corn Exchange, at York, 'under the Wood, presidency of Mr. George Marshall, Grand Master Darling- ton), and the vice-presidency of Mr. Jas. W Deputy, Grand Master (Willaston, near Nantwich.), The_ ftateo present, who hail from all parts of the ,kingdom, number about 170. The business of the day was very brief. `.- The roll having been called, the officers were appointed.- The. meeting was then adjourned for business to Tuesday &tam- ing. During the afternoon most of the delegates attended the gala which, under the auspices of the brethren of the York district, took place in Bootharn, and was inaugurated by a grand procession of brethren in their regalia through the city. The Yorkshire Philosophical Society have kindly opened their beautiful grounds and museum to the delegates without payment for admission.

- - ORDER OF SHEPHERDS. The A.M.C. of the Ancient Order of Shepherds, Ashton Unity, opened a week's conference at Tunstall on Monday morning, under the presidency of the Chief Secretary. Dele- gates representing 01,000 members were present, and satis- factory progress was reported in every department. During the past year 5,319 new members had been enrolled, 47 new lodges opetted,and 4,351 members had died or left the Order, leaving a net gain for the year of 988. During the year £45,237 had been paid for sickness and deaths. The funds of the Order were reported tl be in a most satisfactory con- dition, the present capital being £187,321, being an increase of £13,672 over the sum reported at the A.M.C. last year.— Bro. Jas. Farron, of Ashton, was elected Grand Secretary; Bro. Schofield, of Ashton, was voted to the office of Trea- surer ; and Bro. Archdale, of Ashton, re-appointed Editor of the "Magazine." Bros. Halstead (Tunstall), Brown (Chor- ley), and Halstead (Loveclough), were elected to vacancies on the Board of Management, and Bro. Ashton (Bolton) junior auditor and Parliamentary agent.

- - SONS OF TEMPERANCE. Tbe 26th Annual Session of the National Division of Great Britain and Ireland of this order of total abstainers, was opened in tke Temperance Hall, Rochdale, on Monday, the Most Worthy Patriarch, Brother Norman Macleod, pre- siding. One hundred and fifty delegates were present from London, Manchester, Liverpool, Birmingham, Wolverhamp- ton, Edinburgh, Warrington,Runco.n, Chester, and all parts of the kingdom. The National Division degree was con- ferred on about fifty representatives. The Most Worthy Patriarch's address, stated that arrangements bad been made for introducing the order into Ireland, but the unsettled state of that country had rendered it impossible to proceed further with the project at present. Charters had been granted for Germany, Gibraltar, and Christiania, for the formation of divisions of the Order. The German division was reported to be in full working order. Statist'ca were quoted, showing that the sickness and mortality of the Order had been less than one-half that of the Hearts of Oak Society, and 40 per cent less than that of the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows. Bro. Clarke, the Most Worthy Scribe's report stated that the returns showed a much larger increase than several pre- vious years. He had prep eyed six graduated scales of con- tributions to meet the requirements of different circumstances, and thirteen out of twenty-five districts bad adopted those in preference to their own. He referred to the low death rate in the Order, being 8.19 against 8.84 last year. Thirteen new divisions and four cadet sections had been instituted during the past year. Total number of members 15,253, a gain over last year of 759. Funds: benefit, £33,903 4s. 4d.; management, £2,416 6s. 3d.; benevolent, £574 16s. 7d. ; Grand Division Funeral, £9,174 Ss. 2d. ; management, 375 51. 7d. ; total £46,444 Os. lid.; increase over last year, £3,127 19s. &I. In the afternoon a discussion took place with reference to mission and the extension of the order, and the action of the most worthy patriarch with reference thereto during the past year was unanimously approved of. Subsequently Past High Chief Ruler Thomas Cnnliffe, of the Independent order of Rechabites, the corresponding secretary, and other officials were introduced as a deputation from that order, and heartily welcomed. P.H.C.R. Cunliffe I said they congratulated the officers and delegates assembled I most heartily on the progress their order had made, seeing that their objects were similar. During his term of office he had been pleased to meet their Most Worthy Patriarch on several occasions, and he had found many points• upon which they agreed, and very few upon 'which they differed. (Hear, hear.) One object he tad in view in attending there that day.was to impress upon them the necessity and importance of vital statistics to be presented to the world. (Hear, hear.) He had had the honour of presenting the statistics of their order to Mr. W. E. Forster, showing the better life of the abstainer as compared with the Oddfellows and Foresters, about whom he had not a word to say except that they met in public- louses. They had been able to prove that it was far better to live without drink than with it—(applause)— and if they could add to the 35,000 Rechabites the 15,000 Sons of Temperance, and place before the community the beneficial results of abstainer' lives as shown in those two orders they would be doing much good. (Hear, bear.) There had beat some talk about amalgamation, and he be- lieved it was nearer now than ever—at any rate they could amalgamate to persuade men that it was better to join their orders than a pedlic house society so as to free the country from the curse of the drink traffic. (Applause.) The most worthy Patriarch briefly and appropriately replied, pointing out how the officers of the two orders worked well side by side.—Mrs. Birch presiding sister of the Liverpool Grand Union of Daughters of Temperance, and a number of Rochdale , Daughters of Temperance having been admitted the follow-,j ling address was read:— ' -I

div.p: DAUGHTERS OF TEMPERANCE.

VICTORIA UNION NO. 2. To the most worthy patriarch, officers, and members of the National Division of the Sons of Temperance of Great Britain and Ireland. We, of the Victoria Union Daughtcrs of Temperance, of the oldest organisation in England, on behalf of our noble order, offer to you out most cordial greeting on this, your second visit to our good old town of Rochdale' the birth-place of some noble-minded men. We rejoice that it has fallen to our lot to welcome into our midst an assembly so noble as you are. Because of the work your organisation has and will accomplish in spreading the cause of knowledge and temperance. We think, therefore, that the more we know of your organisation, and the more You know of ours, and the closer we are united, the greater will be the sympathy one for the other that we may draw closer and closer together in the long and continued battle with England's greatest curse, intemperance. Most worthy Patriarch, we thank you for the honour you have conferred upon us by allowing us to be present on this occasion, and trusting thlt you believe us always ready and willing to push forward the great cause that we voluntarily pledge to maintain. , We ask you to accept this address on behalf of the members of our noble union. SARAH ANN IORD, P.S. HANNA LIIND, P.P.S. ELIZABETH BeTTFRWORTII, S JANE JACKSON, P.P.S. JANE MARSH, S. A. HAWTHOHNTHWAITE, PPIPPISSI Rochdale, June Gth, 1881.

IVIIAT SHAIL-VirE DRINK? No doubt the saying from the East that "water is best.e. are words of wisdom; yet all are not of the mind to me water "neat." We are artificial in our tastes and sentiment; and hating to meet prejudices as well as we can, we submit a few recipes to make pleasant and useful substitutes fog those exciting and mischief-making drinks now commonly in use, first premising that the demand for cool and at the same time slightly stimulating beverages is natural, taped.. ally in summer time. Heat causes evaporation from the body, and those who are engaged in active exercise, or who are employed in close rooms, or the open sunshine, require fluid to replace the loss. It should also be remembered that much fluid is a cause of profuse perspiration, and ultimately of thirst. Persons who are always drinking are always thirsty. Water slowly sipped will quench the thirst for far longer period than if taken in large draughts at once. All alcoholics, whether in the form of beer, brandy-and- soda, or wine, or cider, &C., ultimately increase the thirst, injure the liver, and render the drinker liable to sunstroke and other forms of injury to the brain, and nervous system generally. Iced beverages should be indulged in caret ally. Tempting as they are, they are not without danger rand they interfere with digestion by lowering the temperature of the stomach. As a drink for mankind let us specially men• tion pure cool water. A few slices of lemon in water Make a most healthful and refreshing beuerage. The lemon ftiluld be squeezed till most of its juice is mixed with the wafter, and then two or three slices of the peel 150—ad be arded. The acidity and the slight bitterness render the "water thirst-quenching. A good sized lemon or tier.. will flasiour bran gallon of water. Sugar may be added lirmitall critaaa-. titles if desired, but the less the better; or-.boiling water poured on a sliced lemon, sugar added, strained, qind drunk cold, is much approved. Tea, coffeeonadcocoatarealf liked in harvest work, cocoa being the more nutritious. Ten of goad quality, and made good, to which cold water may be added, is a handy and favourite beverage. Travellers-and- sportsmen allow this to be a refreshing drink. Barley water, with slight flavour of lemon, is nice in. health and in sick- ness; and buttermilk, when it can be obtained., For heavy labour, either agricultural or mechanical, nothing is HO SM.* taining as oatmeal drink, in the proportion'of I.lb. of Meal boiled in three gallons of water, to which is added a little brown sugar This may be used either warm or cold, but should be "well shaken before taken," as the oatmeal sub. aides to the bottom. Those who are engaged in work far from home will find oatmeal, stirred into cold water and drunk off Scotch fashion, a good support.

It WasAvident:that if the Opposition were to tatithe plaei orthe Goiternment they had nothing to offer nen' alterbative to the policy they con- demned, save the old policy of secret agreements and *pen eggression, the policy which embarrassed the finances of the pipire, harassed our trade and industry, and threatened to involve us any day in calamity and disaster. The state of affairs in Ireland was due to the Conservative Government's neglect of all remedial legislation at a time when moderate measures would have prevented the troubles which now existed. Twitting the Tory party on their claims 'to be alone competent to conduct' our relations with foreign governments, Mr. Chamberlain said the concert of Europe had been maintained, and it had been powerful enough to effect the settlement of the difficult questions which at one time threatened a renewal of the war in the East, and the influence of England never stoed higher in Europe than it stood at the present moment. The right hon, gentleman at great length defended the policy of the Government in re- gard to the Transvaal settlement. Sir Evelyn Wood, splendid general as be was, had gained more honour by making peace than winning his greatest battle. Home affairs were most important. The Irish, labouring under an Idea of wrong, and being led on by agitators, had now come to the verge of civil war. He hated coercion, and so did his colleague; but so did they hate disorder more. The law must be maintained, and hence the passing of the Coercion Act. Arother remedial measure was now being promoted in the shape of the Land Bill, and on that measure the Government staked their existence. Whatever the result of the bill, he should rejoice to think be had been associated with the best and noblest statesman this country had ever produced. A resolution of confidence in the honourable member was carried.

Government last year. Mr. Gladstone made no promisee which are not amply redeemed in the Land Bill before Parliament. True, the Government has had to contend against another baleful influence beeides that of the implacable rack-renting evicting landlords,—that of a band of Irish revolutionists, who make no secret of their desire to thwart remedial legislation, and to keep the feud :of Irishmen with Englishmen alive until they see an opportunity of destroying the "Union. Does Sir R. Cross imagine that he and his colleagues would not have had the same incendiary anarchists to cope with if the general election had continued them in office ? The Fenian sedition attained its crisis fourteen years ago during the tenure of a Tory Government; and we have not tie least doubt that by this time, if a repressive policy in Ireland had still been pursmed by a Tory Govern- ment kept in power for another term, the disturbance in Ireland would have assumed the awful proportions of a general rebellion. One other example we may select of tie disingenioneness of Sir Richard Cross as an assailant of the Government. It is on the subject of the public finances. He says the estimates of the late Govern- ment for their,last year were under V 32,000,000, that Mr. Bright had said. "that no one is fit to govern who cannot govern on a less sum than that," and the actual expenditure of the Tory Government was £83,000,000 ; but that the estimates for this year which one would have expected the Government would have made lees, amounted to £84,505,000. There Sir Richard Cross stops, and that is what he calls honest criticism on the comparative finance of Liberal and Conservative Governments. Is it really needful to repeat the fasts and to'expose the gross sophistry of this: representation? Did not the late Government leave behind them heapa upon heaps of uncalculated outstanding liabilities ? Was there not a deficit, and a floating debt upon home account to clear away ? Did not they leave unfinished a war with the Afghani, the result of the stupid aggressive pilicy, which the Liberal Government has had to close? Was it not one of the very first of a nuraber if staggering revelations after the fall of the Tory Ministry that there had been a misstatement of the expenjiture on the Afghan war to the astounding &mould of four millions? Was that enormous deficit added to the fourteen millions that war was before known to have cost, left te be provided for somehow by a Liberal Government ? Is it:not the fact that, the burden being :obviously too great to be saddled apon the people of India, the Government have, as in duty bound, had to provide several millions of it out of British taxation as a grant to: India? Mere, has not the insane act of annexation of the Transvaal by the late Government involved the country in an extraor- dinary military expenditure in South Africa to be reckoned by millions P And with all these liabilities to meet, the consequences of the criminttl profligacy of the Government of which Sir R. Cross was a member, and which the Liberal Government has met in the only way that honest statesmen could meet them, by paying them off as quickly as possible, what do our readers think of the fairness of Sir R. Cross, and of the texture of his Tory conscience, when he comes to St. Helens and states only the naked fact that the estimates for this year are a million higher than those of the last year of Tory rule, without so much as naming any of these accumulated Tory debts and deficits which the Liberal Government has to its sorrow inherited? We hope the country will have the benefit of four or five years of Liberal foreign and domestic policy, during which Mr. Gladstone can control the expenditure as he has not had a chance of doing as yet, and if at the end of ,that reasonable then party's v anyty,e Tory critic willthe Liberal i time of trial, there has been no retrenchment, and no reduction v e to lea o f taxation, enethatwe e pro- fessions of economy have been falsified. But not whilst we are paying off the monstrous bills of a set of Tory spendthrifts.

THE speech to which Mr. Healy gave utterance so appropriately on Sunday, at a place called Swords, in county Dublin, is not one that can be said to be remarkable for good sense or good taste. Even its great vulgarity would not have earned notice for it if the member for Wexford had not resolved to strike out a new line by challenging a Minister of the Crown to a duel. Mr. Healy is heartily welcome to the admis- sion that his new method of trying to insult Mr. Forster if not altogether original does less credit to his inventive honours than some others which he and his friends have chosen. These persons can scarcely be expected to be troubled by anything that may be said about the breach of good manners of which one .an is guilty who applies an offensive epithet to another. Perhaps they may be more concerned if some one assists them in understanding that whoever was the irst to associate Mr. Forster's name with the soubriquet '" Buckshot" invented a miserably poor joke, and that whoever repeats it gives stronger proof of his own vulgarity than of his originality. Whilst Mr. Healy made such a poor display of manners and wit on this as on most other occasions, one can scarcely fail to notice his great prudence. It was an emi- nently safe thing for a member of his stamp to invite a man of Mr. Forster's to "cross the Channel to other lands" to those unnamed but plainly iudicatei countries "to which it would not be quite so safe" for the Chief Secretary to invite him to go as to Ire- land. No one in the world, and least of all the man who gave it, would ever believe that there was the remotest probability of such a challenge being ac- cepted. Mr. Healy could therefore give the challenge with full respect for his own skin, knowing that he did not in any degree endanger its safety by inviting Mr. Forster to cross swords with him. Whether the Chief Secretary and his colleagues will consider that such a speech entitles Mr. Healy to any other attention than being severely let alone remains to be seen. It is quite possible that it will be held to contain not only a breach of manners, but a breach of Parliamentary privilege as well. There is one objection against such a way of dealing with the incident, and that is that it would bring into prominence a person of whom the least that is said even in depreciation the better. We have no doubt Mr. Forster stands in need of all the philosophy he can command in order to disregard the vulgar malevolence of the unscrupu- lous attacks that are daily being made upon him. We have long noticed in these attacks something entirely distinct from even the worst passions of controversy. Political fanaticism of the worst slags —such fanaticism, for instance, as that which animates revolutionists in most countries and which is more akin to mania than to vice—is less offensive than the forma which the hostility of the Irish Irreconcileables sometimes take. The fanaticism which moves continental agitators has often a very broad istellectual basis. There is nothing mean in it, nothing vulgar, nothing deliberately offensive. It is often nothing more than political philosophy gone mad, and against such a thing as that society can always protect itself. Now, there is a noteworthy absence of fanaticism in the politicians who are giving Mr. Forster so much trouble. Their vice mofaythreelyaguitpaotnor it tf motive qualities are more objectionable than that pet We that coannmtreines.ofsatvhee stamp of Healy were animated. by "illy Mr. Timothy Michael of the revolutionary character, etphietaint of the higher, though not less givteoruoulds,niomt impulses their breath in casting state at d members lof the Government or in offering silly a insincere formed en of mustt h provocation to statesmen whom they well k not respond to them. Very low indeed thenwill be the best estimate that can be faction, even when an effort is made to determinelll what place should be assigned to them amongst the revolutionists of "pure blood." There is but little reason to fear, however, that even Mr. Healy Hhould require special measures to be taken on his account. Vulgarity, and impertinence after all

are not of themselves dangerous forces, and so long as his wit shows itself only in repeating epithets which others have coined, and in offering challenges which no one will accept, he will not be such a very terrible personage.

Tun Board of Trade returns for the last month are happily calculated to afford consolation and hope to those who have been fearing that the recent revival of trade was temporary, and that already a reaction had commenced. Both the imports and exports show a substantial increase over the corresponding period of last year. The imports last month were valued at £32,821,942, and the exports at £19,087,648, compared with £30,453,114 and £17,277,876 for the month of May last year, or an increase in the imports of £2,368,828, and in the exports an increase of £1,809,772, and this over a month, when it will be remembered the hopes of a revival were greatest. This does not appear to corroborate in the slightest degree the statement that our commercial affairs are going from bad to worse as some people would have us believe. Compared with two years ago, there is an increase of £5,154,289 in our iraports, or about 16 per cent. Our imports of raw cotton show a consider- able increase, and whilst there is a slight decrease in the imports of raw silk, this is amply made up for by the very decided increase which has taken place in the imports of raw wool. We must confess that it is very difficult to reconcile the continuous increase in our imports of raw wool, with the gloomy reports of the conditions of the English woollen trade. During the first five months of 1879 we imported 265,000,0001b5. of wool; last year it increased to 287,000,0001b5., and this year it ha's reached nearly 304,000,0001b5. The school of political economists, who believe in " exports " rather than imports as an indication of prosperity, will be gratified to notice that the exports for last month exceeded those of May, 1880, by nearly two millions, and those of May, 1879, by more than two millions and a half. Unfortunately, the returns as to the iron trade are not so satisfactory as we should like. There is a decrease in iron, but not more than or even as much as might have been expected from the reaction from undue activity, and there is still an increase in the export of steel and cast or wrought iron. With the exception of woollen manufactures generally, most of the other leading articles show a decided increase, and, taken altogether, the figures must be regarded as very satisfactory. It is rather remarkable as a practical comment on much that is said respecting the alleged decadence of British manufactures, and the undue, as it is said, increase of imports, that in the five months of 1881, the imports have decreased five millions compared with those of 1880, but that the exports have increased nearly a million and a half.

not understood literally by the commentators and Christian teachers of the nineteenth cen- tury. The general may be a good man, but his followers who neglect to remember the advice of Solomon that money answereth all things, and band over to such an enthusiastall their spare coin, may, notwithstanding their faith in Provi- dence, find themselves applying to the relieving officer if they are attacked by a severe illness. It seems to me very bad policy to interfere in such a serious manner with any of the officers of the corps who have in the past tried to do their duty, because they happen to smoke in moderation. It is very much to be regretted that the St. John's Ambulance Society movement has not been taken up in this district I hear that in one town the movement has not only been taken up by a large number of ladies, but that the police have joined it, and many of them have passed satisfactory examinations. A little surgical knowledge is no doubt of , advantage to a policemen as well as to other men. "Robert " is not only exposed to dangers himself, but he is often the first summoned to a serious accident, or some other dreadful occurrence, where one or more human lives may depend upon some timely treatment, even though it be of the.simplest character. Not long ago a man was run over by a very heavy wagon. The poor fellow's leg was broken, and whilst a cab was.being fetched a police-sergeant who arrived promptly on the scene, obtained a broom handle and his staff, and used these contrivances for splints. The leg was bound up by the time the vehicle arrived to convey the man home. The officer had received ambulance instruction, and was at any rate able to make practical use of it. I ;Incerely hope that some one will take the matter up, and that the movement will be heartily encouraged for the benefit of suffering humanity. Another American psychological phenomenon has appeared. A New York lady claims to be able to read large Print with her eyes tightly bandaged! She is said to be enabled to do it by means of an electric light thrown from the back of her brain. I have heard of people having prodigiously large beads, but never of a human being whose cranium conld hold a Brush, candle, and a Gramme Machine!

Mr. Thomas Norman, and Mr. Philip Speakman have, within the last few days, received a communication from the Local Government Board to the effect that a certain sum charged by them as expenses whilst visiting London, will not be allowed unless the Board are provided with vouchers, showing how the money was expended. These two worthy gentlemen decided that it was imperatively necessary th it if they were to attain their commendable object of getting the railway fares from Liverpool to Runcorn reduced, they must take the opportunity which offered of personally inter- viewing one of the great railway magnates at Ruston Station, London. They succeeded in getting a pass for the two, and it never seems to have entered their minds that the Local Government Board would decline to sanction their charge of about 30s. each for personal expenses, as they were on important ratepayers' business, and proved successful in the object for which they visited the metropolis. But the Local Government Board with a paternal curiosity which must be very irritating, desire to know where the £3 went. FLACCUS.

YEOMANRY INTELLIGENCE.—The London Gazette states that Second-Lieutenant George Henry Hugh Earl of Rocksavage, resigns his commission in the Cheshire Yeomanry Cavalry. CHOIR TRIP FROM IttrwcouN.—The choir of Greenway- road Chapel, Runcorn, chose this year to spend a day at Windermere, and they succeeded in passing a very pleasant day. Mr. Billingsley, organist and conductor, was in charge and made the necessary arrangements, and it is needless to say that they were all that could be desired. BELLAINGING AT RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH.—Eight members of the Lancashire Association of Change Ringers met at All Saints' Parish Church, Runcorn, the other day, and rang a half peal of grandsire triples, consisting of 2,500 changes, Hotta Tenpart, in one hour and thirty minutes. Ist S. Gough, 2nd J. Davison, 3rd W. Beacall, 4th J. Large, sth H. Turner, 6th G. W. Hughes, 7th J. Aspinwall, Bth J. Leadbetter. Tenor 16 cwt. Conducted by J. Aspinwall. - GOOD TirsarLARISM. —The quarterly council of the Juvenile Templar Order of South-West Lancashire was held on Saturday, at Earlestewn. The meeting was called to order by Sister Green, D.S.J.T., there being present repre- sentatives from Earlestown, St. Helens, Garston, Warring- ton, Liverpool, dm. The D.S.J.T. reported thirty-two temples in working order. The district treasurer reported a substantial balance in hand, and the reports of the visiting superintendents and superintendents of temples showed the Juvenile Order to be in a prosperous condition, and assistance in the working of the temples was again urgently requested. At the last council held in Liverpool, it was re- solved, en the motion of Brother Skaife, to send a memorial to our city and county M.P.'s respecting the present mode of dealing with youthful offenders; and Sister Green reported having douse so, and read replies received from Lord Sandon, Lord C. Hamilton. Sir R. A. Cross, Lieut.-Col. I. Blackburne, and Mr. Edward Whitley, written in a kind and courteous manner, acknowledging the receipt of the memo- rial and expressing sympathy with its object; the reading of the letters calling forth hearty applause from all present. After partakingof a substantial tea, the meeting re-assembled, and resolved to hold its next council at Garston. A public meeting was afterwards held, presided over by Bro. Lindon, of St. Heleus, when addresses were given by Sister Green, D.S.J.T., and Bro. Reid, D.T., being enlivened by songs and recitations given by the members of the Pride of Earlestown Juvenile Temple.

ATHLETIC SPORTS AT WAREINOTON.—Abont a thou- sand persons assembled on Whit-Monday in the field opposite the post office, to witness the athletic sports of the work- people engaged at the Dallam and Bewsey forges of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company. The weather was fine to the conclusion of the last race, when the rain which had been threatening for some hours, commenced to fall, and put out of question the dancing that was antici- pated, the music for which was to have been furnished by the Volunteer band, which, under the conductorship of Mr. Newns, played an admirable selection of pieces during the afternoon. We reret to state that the sports were con- ducted in such a manner as to provoke much unfavourable criticism from the spectators. For about an hour from the commencement of the sports everything went on smoothly, but while preparations were being made for the second event on the programme those who had paid something extra to be apart from the "vulgar herd " were alarmed to see the latter rushing about the course in all directions, and an— noyed to see them take possession of every part of the field Other than that to which they had paid for admission. When the tug of war was announced many of the spectators I were utterly bewildered as to the number of teams in the contest, for nearly all the forgemen present swarmed round the officials and appeared to be preparing to take off their coats. The event had to be postponed for a while, and at this iuncture the arrival of several policemen had a wonder- ful effect upon the onlookers, who were kept in order for the remainder of the afternoon by the men in blue. For the 120 yards at race handicap there were 40 entries, and the the event was run in 10 heats, the winners of which were—lst heat, W. Hough, 10 yards; 2nd, G. Beards, 19k; 31d, R. Tickle. 26; 4th, J. Walsh, ; sth, T. McGuiness, 161 ; 6th, R. Dumbell, 19; 7th, W. Massey, 191; Bth, J. Fogg, 18k; 9th, J. Sankey, 19; 10th, •J. Kilduff, 20. The second round reduced the competitors to three—Hough, J. Walsh, and G. Beards, who in the final heat secured the following places :-1, J. Walsh, prize £2 10s.; 2, W. Hough, £1 109. ; 3, G. Beards, 15s. There were 13 entries for the two mile walking handicap, but only six men turned out. The scratch man Langall, who walked in capital style, soon overhauled his opponents, some of whom were as tall again as himself, and amid cheers came in easily first man. let prize, £1 108., J. Lan,gall (scratch) •, 2, 155., T. May, 300 yards ; 3,7 s. 6d., J. Cartwright, GOO yards. Some dissatisfaction was caused by the mile handi- cap, it being contended that the competitors did not run the full distance. T. Walsh with 140 yards start ran well and looked like winning many people being of opinion that another lap had to be run, but the result was announced as follows :-1, £1 10s., J. Rowson, 300 yards; 2, 155., T. Dainty, 220; 3,7 s. 6d., B. Thomason, 150. In the tug of war the Bewsey team (captain Bradbury) beat the Hallam team (captain Lee) twice out of three trials, and were de- clared the winners of the prize £l. The first prize for the half-mile handicap was £1 10s., the second 155., and the third 7s. 61' and seven men turned out for the event, which was won by 3. Rawson, 150 yards; 2, W. Hough, 30; 3, T. Walsh, 60. G. and E. Allen, 17 yards start, secured the first prize of 15s. in the three legged race, the second, 58., being carried off by J. Atherton and J. Sankey. Of the 15 iris° had entered for the quarter-mile handicap 13 put in an appearance, and the event proved the best contested of the afternoon. J. Walsh, 45 yards start, came in winner of the let prize, £2; while Hough, the last man, with 5 yart',l start, passed his men in admirable style and secured the second prize, £1; the third, 10s., falling to G. Beards% with 45 yards start.

Arms/Prim SurcinE IA BOT.—At the Manchester County ,Police-court, on Tuesday before Sir John Mantel], a lad of of 13 years, living in Buckley-street, Newton Heath, was charged on remand with having attempted to commit suicide. On Sunday week last the lad was told to go to school, but did not do so. On his return home he was ordered upstairs, and soon after was found attempting to hang himself. When questioned as t@ his motive, he replied that he was ashamed of himself for not going to school. Sir John Islantel I now sent him for trial at the sessions. TIIE LATE IiATCTI BETWEEN LANCASIIIIIE AND NOT- TINGHAMSIIIIIE.-It is pleasing to notice that W. Marriott, the professional to the Huyton Cricket and Bowling Club, I was chosen as one of the representatives of the Notts county I team in the match against LanCashire, at Manchester, on Thursday and Friday last. There is reason to believe that his services were fully satisfactory to, and appreciated by, the committee of the Notts county. In the first innings he scorced 13, and in the second 14 in addition to which he did good service with the ball, bowling five overs at a cost of ten runs and two wickets. Taken on the whole, this is really , good work. considering the team the Notts county had pitted ' against them. • -

THE CHanwicx ESTATE.— Nearly all our neigh- bouring towns in Lancashire have had a millionaire, and some people have gone so far as to claim £18,000,000 of Sir Andrew Chadwick's estate. We are informed that Mr. Jos. Chadwick, of Unsworth, near Bury, has of late come to the conclusion that he is the heir-at-law Of Sir Andrew Chad- wick, and has filed a bill to that effect. Mr. Joseph Chad- wick claims all the real estate of Sir Andrew, let it be worth £lB,OOO or £18,000,000. Messrs. Bradford and Farish, of 70, Queen Victoria-street, London, E.C., have been employed on behalf of Joseph Chadwick, and if the court will give them a hearing they feel confident, with the evidence they have in their possession, they can convince any court that Joseph Chadwick is the lawful heir to thelong-contested estate of Sir Andrew Chadwick.—Bury Times. ASSEMBLING OF THE 2ND ROYAL LANCASHIRE lILT.ITIA. —On Monday and Tuesday the 2nd Royal Lancashire Militia came up for their annual training. The men as- sembled at the Orford Barracks where they received their clothing and accoutrements, and left the same evening by Special trains per London and North Western Railway, for the camp at Altcar, whither the recruits proceeded last week. Of the conduct of the recruits the Chief Constable spoke in complimentary terms at the Borough Court, on Tuesday, Mr. Hunt remarking that until that morning not a single member of the 2nd Militia had appeared before the Bench this year. A Liverpool contemporary, after stating that the regiment is about to become the 3rd and 4th (or Militia) Battalions of "The Liverpool Regiment," says:— The 2nd Lancashire was raised towards the end of last century, and did permanent duty during the Peninsular War, forming part of the militia force which volunteered for foreign service and landed in France as the Battle of 'Toulouse (April 10th, 1814), the last engagement of the war, was being fought. The regiment was disembodied after the „European peace, and do not appear to have been assembled again more than once or twice between the period of Waterloo and the date of the militia revival in 1852. Previous te the latter year the last time the 2nd Lancashire were called out appears to have been about the years 928 or 1830, when they drilled in the Pumptields, Vauxhall- road. In 1852, 1853, and 1854, the regiment was called up for 28 days drill each year, and in the latter year were pre- sented with new colours, which had to be put away the very next year, when the corps was converted into riflemen. The change of uniform took place in Glasgow, where, in 1855 and 1856, the regiment performed permanent duty, returning to Liverpool for disembodiment in the latter year. The corps will soon be clothed hi red coats once more, this training being their last appearance as rifles. THE LATE SUNDAY SCHOOL CENTENARY CELEBRA- TION IN WARRINGTON.—The friends of the Sunday school movement in Warrington will be gratified to learn that the Centenary Committee, after paying all expenses incurre I in the celebration, have a balance in hand of a few pounds. In consequence of this, a meeting of the committee was held in Wycliffe schoolroom on Friday evening last to decide how the funds should be appropriated. The unanimous feeling of the meeting was that as far as possible the money should be spent in accordance with the wishes of the contri- butors, and eventually it was resolved to arrange for a grand concert of sacred music, similar to the one given last August in the Public Hall, to take place about October next, for the purpose of raising sufficient money to present each school which joined the Warrington celebration, according to the number of scholars, with a percentage of copies of the revised ' edition of the New Testament, such copies to be the property of each school, and to contain a suit- able inscription as a memorial of the Centenary. The officers were unanimously reappointed as follows : chairman, Mr. Mathew Bowden; treasurer' Mr. John Hall; secretary, Mr. Win. Roberts. It was also decided to invite Messrs.:F. M. Pattison, and J. Muir, who so kindly gave their services on the last occasion, to again place them at the dis- posal of the committee. The object aimed at we are sure will meet with general approval, as it will not only relieve the schools of a financial difficulty, in procuring the revised edition of the New Testament for the use of their schools, but it will also established in the school a lasting memorial of the Sunday School Centenary MARRIAGE OF MISS SUNSIERSGILL, OF SANKEY BRIDGES —Sankey Bridges was on Saturday both lively and joyous, Owing to the marriage of Miss Summersgill to Mr. J. S. Snoddy, schoolmaster, of Widnes. At an early hour flags were hoisted on the grounds in front of the Wesleyan Chapel, and several cottages hung flags out of their windows. A large number of the villagers were present at Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel, Warrington, where the ceremony was conducted by the Rev. J. R. Berry, of Liverpool, formerly minister at Warrington. Among those present at the marriage were :—Mr. Summersgill (father of the bride), Misses Polly and Maggie Sammersgill (sisters of the bride), Miss Snoddy (Longhop,, Gloucestershire), Miss Minnie Goldsmith (Isle of Man), and MISS Hallam (Timperley) ; Mr. Thomas Snoddy (Heckmondwike), Mr. W. Snoddy (Pembroke Dock), Mr. J. Summersgill (Heywood), Mr. J. Newby (Middleton), and Mr. Peers Marsh (Warrington). Numerous presentations were made including a handsome tea urn, with the following inscription:—" Presented to Miss Summersgill, on the occasion of her marriage, by the teachers of the Sankey Bridges Sunday school, June 4th, 1881," accompanied with an illuminated address, as an ex- pression of their esteem and desire for her future welfare. A water colour painting of" Bolton Abbey" (Yorkshire) in gold frame; family Bible commentary, by Henry and Scott illustrated; damask table cloth, silver dinner cruet, silver tea spoons, breakfast cruet, bedroom service, glass engraved biscuit box, two sets of china tea services, large quantity of cut and engraved glass, dtc., drc. In the afternoon the newly-married couple took leave of their friends and pro- ceeded per rail to Windermere.

COUNII RIFLE CONTEST LT ALTCAIL—The 21st annual prize meeting of the county of Lancaster Rifle Association commenced on Saturday, on the commodious shooting range at Altcar. The departure from the custom of holding the meeting at the latter end', of Whit-week instead of the days as at present arranged has not materially decreased the number of entries, though it has not had the effect of adding to the number of competitors. There is an increase in some instances and a falling off in others, so that the aggregate number remains about the same as last year. In order to avoid any scandal with respect to marking, Mr. Spencer, the treasurer and secretary, who also undertakes the office of executive officer, had adopted the plan of changing the letters at each firing point after the completion of everylcompetition, thus preventing any collusion between the register keepers and markers, as no one knows until the moment of firing at what letter he pray be squadded at. For the Members' Snider Prizes there were 156 entries, as compared with 140 last year; for the Any Rifle Derby Com- petition 8 entries, against 13 last year; for the Legh Chal- lenge Cup 266 entries, as compared with 291 last year; the Cotton Brokers' Prize (open to all corners) 262, last year 301; the Martini-Henry (in two stages) 90, last year 87; the Tilney Challenge Prize 24, last year 31; the Nursery Prize 163, last year 156; the Lord Lieutenant's Prize 282, last year 288; the Artillery Carbine Prize 81, last year 115 ; Yeomanry and Light Horse Prizse 25, last year 54 ; the Engineer and Naval Artillery Prizes 35, last year 54 ; the Battalion Challenge Cup 5, last year 7 ;volley prizes 11, last year 17; Grand Challenge Cup and the bronze medals of the National Rifle Association, with badges of the County of Lancaster Rifle Association, 185 entries, last year 192. div.head: LOCAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL NOTES.

At the last meeting of the Widnes Local Board several tenders were considered for the flagging of Simm's Cross Board Schools. Mr. Beasley (law clerk) remarked that since the matter had been entered into and decided upon by the Highway Committee, he had received a communication from Mr. Hirst, the gentleman who had been successful in having his tender accepted at £6lO, stating that he could not undertake it under £648. The plan of altering tenders after it has become known what was the highest amount asked, next to the one accepted, is a pretty old one, and it would be very unfair to the other tradesmen to give Mr. Hirst the preference under such peculiar circumstances. At the same meeting the Chairman (Major Cross) drew the attention of the members to a very important matter, viz., that unless the sewerage scheme were proceeded with p-io- to the Ist July they were under a bond to pay £2,312. Sooner or later the work of se,vering the town will have to be gone on with, and I understand that the Chairman in- tends to bring the question forward for full deliberation at the meeting on Tuesday next. It is a very serious matter to have to consider the possibility of forfeiting between £2,000 and £3,000 for not carrying out the work within a specified time, but there is no doubt that the ratepayers will view with considerable alarm any proposal to spend such a considerable sum as the execution of sewerage works would cost at a time when trade is in such a depressed state as at present in Widnes. A story is going about the town of Runcorn to the effect that a townsman who is somewhat noted for his foresight in a business point of view, has, within the last few days done a good stroke ef business. In a certain part of Ruucorn there lives a wealthy gentleman, and opposite to his resi- dence are two rather fice houses which were put up for sale. An offer was made to dispose of them to the gentleman in question, but he declined to pay the sum asked, on the ground that the buildings were not worth the money. They were then put before the property buyer referred to, and he became a purchaser. One may imagine the chagrin of the opulent gentleman on hearing that the buyer intended to convert the houses into shops ! The prospect of having two shops for an outlook caused the gentleman to make the pro- perty owner an offer for the buildings, but it was only accepted on condition of his paying £5OO as the price of his bargain !

A preliminary appeal against the surcharges of the auditor upon the members of the Widnes Board has been forwarded to•the Local Government Board. In the wee short hour ayont the twal of ons of the morn- ings of this week, Dr. McDougall, of Runcorn, and "a dis- tinguished party," paid a visit to most of the lodging houses of the town. They saw many sad and some few amusing scenes. Some of the poor wretches were, no doubt, in their strange lodgings owing to the worship they have paid to "Inspiring, bold John Barleycorn." Let us hope that as they saw so sorry a collection of their fellow creatures, they were inclined to say—quoting again from "Bobbie " ~ Then gently scan your brother man, Still gentler, sister woman; Though they may gang a rennin' wrong, 'To step aside Is human." Probably, my friend the doctor is getting up the mattrials of a graphic speech on the lodging house question, upon which I may say he is no mean authority. Your faithful correspondent had the irrepressible oath question thrust before him in a queer and somewhat novel form at a county court the other day. A man applied to the judge for the committal of a debtor who had failed to com- ply with a judgment summons. His Honour put the usual question as to whether the plaintiff was prepared to swear that the defaulter was able to pay. The plaintiff hesitated, and Hie judge plainly told him that he could not make the order unless he was able to swear that the defendant could pay. There was another long pause, when suddenly the silence was broken by a shrill voice crying out from the back of the court, "Why don't you swear, you old fool." The result was a burst of laughter, which was quickly sup- pressed, but the possessor of the shrill voice did not reveal herself. It was in vain that the judicial eye roamed over the court in search for the disturber of the proceedings. I may be wrong, hut I have a shrewd impression, that it was the old gentleman's wife, who was simply coming to her husband's rescue when he was struggling with his con- scientious scruples.

The members of the branch of the Salvation Army in Runcorn do not yet appear to have given in their entire adherence to the proposition of their captain that they should cease smoking. It seems that the leader and a few others of the band have entirely abandoned the use of the fragrant weed, and they are not inclined to become martyrs themselves without making others follow their example. What injury is likely to result to the work by some of their members declining to put their tobacco and catty-pipes on what is called "the altar" is a mystery to people outside the charmed circle. Surely, a man may be God-fearing and anxious to do his duty who takes a pipe after a hard day's work. I have theught over the proposal of the captain, and I beg to make him a suggestion to the effect that it is not absolutely necessary that he should have butter to his bread, or many other creature comforts in which I am told hissoul delighteth, but if he carries his argument to its legitimate issue, lam afraid he will land himself in a quandary. Paul says it is not well to eat meat nor anything whereby a " brother' may be made to stumble or become weak, and also that he that giveth the maid in marriage doeth well, but he that giveth her not in marriage doeth better. Perhaps some of the fair ones connected with the Army may be of the same opinion as the young lady whose father wrote this passage in her Bible. She, with that quickness of perception which characterises the sex, wrote underneath it, "Let ma- de well—let those who like do better." Marriage, accord- ing to the Apostle, was not a necessity except to certain men, and there is no doubt that in many cases it is a very expensive luxury. Fine houses and broad cloth are not absolutely necessary, but are Christians called upon to become miserable and to debar themselves of nearly every creature comfort, if connected with the Salvation Army, in order to hand all their spare cash to General Booth, with- out doubting ? Prudence and the faculty of saving have been implanted in men so that they may make a provision for a rainy day, and not be kicked from pillar to post if they happen to be out of a berth for a few weeks. All men are not called upon to live merely by faith in temporal matters, and the command that if a man had two coats he was to
