STATE OF IRELAND.

The Rev. Engine Spechy, whl was arrested under the Coercion Act, and lodged in Naas Gaol, has been removed from his cell to the Infirmary on account of b illness and placed under the care of a nurse. A force of one hundred police proceeded to Cappa, County Armagh, yesterday, to protect a bailiff in evicting a tenant on the estate of Mrs. Hagan. The proceedings passed off quietly.

div.head: MORE RIOTING IN CORK.
div.p: MORE RIOTING IN CORK.

A correspondent telegraphing on Thursday night, says Serious rioting is proceedieg in Cork this evening. It originated in one of the drinking tents of the racecourse with a row. The police were called to stop the disturbance, and, having made an arrest, a prisoner was after a good deal of stone-throwing, rescued from twelve policemen. The helmets of the police were stbashed, their heads cut, and their bodies bruised in several parts. They, however, suceeeded in making another arrest, but at the entrance to the Park Racecourse the civilian power became so overwhelming that they were obliged to let their prisoner go, netwithstanding that at this point they were reinforced by twelve mounted men. The crowd when in closecontact with them beat the police with blackthorn sticks, and the police returned the attack with the butts of their muskets, knocking down all who came within their „reach. In the meantime the stones thrown by

such of the crowd as kept at a safer distance fell Oen the police as thick as hail. One policeman got a severe stab in the thigh, and a civilian had his head split open from the -blow of a musket, lie is reported dead. Soldiers leaving the course. were stoned, and the foot and mounted police

continued to charge at the point of the bayonet the crowd into the city. At Anglesea Bridge, the first cross thomughfare met with, the police were hemmed in and attacked whilst passing over the bridge front and rear. The mounted men with drawn swords charged the mob, trampled on such as could not escape, and wounded many with bayonets. A cessation of hosilities for half an hour took place; after this the police, whilst in the meantime endeavouring to snatch a hasty meal, had to leave their table owing to the showers of stones hurled at them from across the river, coming through their windows. Captain Stokes and Mr. Mitchell, resident magistrates, who were at the time in barracks, the former wounded by a stone, ordered the police out once more; and whilst they were, to the number of 120, drawn up in front of the barracks, on Union Quay, their line was more than once broken by stones thrown at them across the river. The crowd were charged and dispersed through narrow streets at the point of the bayonet, but only to assemble again and renew their attack on the police.. One mounted man was knocked off his horse

and seriously injured. The streets are rapidly filling with rowdies, and all respectable citizens are quickly getting in doors. The military are being called out in expectation of a bad night. Already upwards of twenty arrests have been I made, some of them brought to bridewell at the point of r revolvers. One policeman in plain clothes who drew his revolver on the crowd, and declared he would shoot the first man who attempted to rescue a prisoner he had just detected throwing a stone, was beaten to the ground with sticks, but he brought his prisoner down with him, and held on until the mounted men rode down his assailants. Fearful excite- ment prevails.
• FORTY SUFFERERS IN THE INFIRMARY. Over 40 civilians were treated early yesterday morning at the Cork Infirmary, for injuries received in last night's
rioting The majority were scalp wounds, but one man Itad his leg broken. It is reported that Sub-constable lkl‘Gowan . . . . . .
was stabbed by a man who carried a long stick with a piece of iron heop at the end. The town is now quiet.
THE IRISH MILITIA AND THEIR BOUNTY.

The Secretary of State for War has issued instructions regarding the payment of bounty to non-commissioned officers and men of the Irish Militia. All such as were enlisted or re-enlisted prior to 2nd March last, and effective on April Ist, will be paid their annual bounty in the same manner as if their regiments had assembled for training. Men who may not be forthcoming when the general pay- ments take place may be paid on subsequent application, except under special circumstances. Men who have become non-effective since April Ist, or who have volunteered for the regular army, will be paid.

div.head: VICTORIA CROSS.
div.p: THE VICTORIA CROSS.

A Royal warrant has been issued to define the qualifica- tions for the decoration of the Victoria Cross. The quali- fication is to be conspicuous by bravery or devotion to the country in the presence of the enemy, and it is Her Majesty's further will and pleasure that officers and men of the military and reserve forces—naval and military—should be eligible for that decoration under these conditions.
THE DUKE OF DEVONSHIRE AND HIS IRISH TENANTS. The Duke of Devonshire has allowed the members on his
Irish estates a reduction of 10 per cent, off their half year's rent, due this month.
DIABOLICAL ATTEMPT TO BLOW UP THE LIVERPOOL AWN RAIL.

The suspicions of two constables and a cabman, who were close to the Town Hall, at four o'clock yesterday morn- ing, were excited by the appearance of two men, who were standing on the steps of the Town Hall at the west door. They had with them what appeared to be a large sailor's canvas bag. They suddenly left it at the door and ran away. Police-constable 884 went up to the door and found the bag there. He states that he heard something fizzing inside, and he pulled it away from the door, and threw it into the middle of the street opposite Brown's-building. He had just time to shout to his brother constable (898), " clear out," and they had fallen back a few yards, when a terrific explosion took place, and the street was filled by a blinding volume of smoke. The two constables at once ran after the men they had seen running across the Exchange Flags. The men made for Oldhall-street, and the constables followed, blowing their whistles. The signall attracted the attention of Police- constable 553, who was on duty in Oldhall-street, and he succeeded in catching one of them, named M‘Kavitt, as he passed. M.Kavitt threw a revolver over a wall close to, and it has since been recovered. The constable having handed M‘Kavitt over to the other two constables who were following, gave chase to the other man, named Barton Roberts, who, however, had a start of a couple of hundred yards. He ran into Leeds-street, and jumped on board a flat. The con- stable followed, and searched one or two other flats cost to. At last, when he got on board the fiat where Roberts was, the latter either jumped or fell into the water in his attempt to escape. The constable managed to get hold of him and to drag him out dripping with the oozy mud and water of the canal. The two other constables quickly came up in answer to the whistle, and both prisoners were safely taken to the detective office. The two men in custody are unquestionably associated with the Fenian movement. M`Kavitt belongs to Warren Point, Ireland, but he says that he has more recently been in New Orleans. The ether, Barton Roberts, is a Scotch- man, speaking with a broad Scotch accent, but he comes of Trish parentage. He also comes from America, having arrived recently in the Arizona. Since his arrival he has been living in Cottenham-street, Kensington. Both men when captured had revolvers upon them and papers connect- ing them with the Fenian movement. One of them was said to have a document in his possession in which par- ticular reference is made to O'Donovan Rossa.

The official police report issued last night states that P.C. 712 about four o'clock this morning observed two men de- posit a package against the west door ot the Town Hall and run away. He gaw the lighted fuse attached but gave chase, informing another constable on his way of the existence of the package. This officer, P.C. 884, with great plack re- moved the sack to the middle of the road where it exploded. WKavitt was captured in a street by the canal side hiding under a lurry with a loaded revolver in his hand. He was handed over to another constable, and after some searching the second .nan was found hiding in a barge upon the canal, having a revolver in his band at full cock. At the police station both men were searched, and upon them documents were found which the report concludes provea without doubt that both men are members of the Fenian organisa- tion, and not only were documents found upon them b Fenian medals. The piping used was a piece ot water main five inches internal diameter.

div.head: SHOCKING SMALLPDX FATALITY.
div.p: SHOCKING SMALLPDX FATALITY.

Mr. Thomas Chastney, pictun dealer, dec., Salford and Blackburn, died last night from smallpox, from which be had been suffering for a Week. Two young men named Norman recently succumbed to the same disease, one of them leaving been taken ill immediately after his return from London, and his two brothers and the young woman to whom he was engaged to be married taking it from him. THE TRANSVAAL DEPUTATION. The Transvaal deputation consists of Mr. White, editor of the Transvaal Argus, and Mr. Lechzman, a loyal Boer, to express to the British Government the universal disfavour with which recent events in the Transvaal is regarded, ha, nrived in London.
LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

r PROGRESS OF TRH LAND BILL.—MI. OLALsTONE, reply. • ing to Mr. O'Kelly, said that if more progress was made than hitherto with the Land Bill at morning sittings, no occasion would exist for demanding urgency. In case it was not so fortunate, it might become necessary to make a further proposal to the House. THE DIABOLICAL OUTRAGE AT LIVERPOOL. Mr. ARNOLD asked if the Government had received any informa- tion as to the reported explosion at the Town Hall, Liver- pool.—Sir W. HARCOURT said he had received a telegram from the Mayor of Liverpool, stating that this morning a lighted fuse was discovered, burning near the door of the Town Hall, and that a constable saw two men leave the spot. He went to the fuse, and found it attached to a parcel like a sailor's bag. He heard a noise in the bag and pulled it into the middle of the road, and then an explosion occurred, breaking the windows of the Town Hall and sur- rounding houses. The bomb which exploded was found to be of the same description, as that which exploded at the police station. Suenv.—The House then went into Committee of Supply on the civil service estimates. Votes for salaries of the officers of the Houses of Parliament and the Treasury were agreed to. On the vote for the Home Office a discussion arose as to the appointment of inspectors of factories and mines.—Sir W. HARCOURT said he had appointed a member elf the artizan class to an inspectorship of mines, and the result of the experiment remained to be seen.—The votewas agree. d to—On the vote for the Foreign Office, Mr. RYLAjqD. complained of the greet cost of the department.— He pointed out the enormous charge for telegraphing, the great disparity which existed as regarded the salaries of the Queen's, Home, and Foreign Office messengers. The former cost ought to be reduced and the latter salaries equalized. —Sir C. DILICE said he hoped next year the charge for telegraphing would be reduced. One of the reasons for the present large expense was telegrams to Chilia and Peru, which coat £1 ss. and £1 6s. per word. The salaries com- plained of had been equalized from new appointments,— Mr. Rmisms condemned the manner in which the Secret Service money of the Foreign Office was managed. He objected to the permanent Under Foreign Office Secretary receiving £3OO in addition to a salary of £2,000 per annum simply for managing the Secret Service Fund,—Lord R. Canncanz, said the Secret Service Fund in other departments was managed without cost. He moved the reduction of the vote by £300; the amount paid to the Foreign Office official for his manage- ment of the fund.—Mr, MITCHELL HENRY condemned the petty opposition that was being raised en the estimates. Its object was clearly to defeat the passing of the Land Bill.—Sir C. OILIER epposol the reduction moved, and de- fended the manner in which the Secret Service money was managed.—Mr. LABOUCHERE said that when he was attache at Constantinople be recollected a Foreign Office messenger bringing a box of pills to Sir H. Bulwer, and his expenses were £420. (Laughter.)—Per the reduced vote' 21; against, 165; majority, 144.—A long discussion ensued as to trans- mitting despatches by post and the expenses of printing and book binding in the office.—Sir C. DILE& explained various details and said the cott of printing and binding were occasioned by the necessity of employing persons of high character as documents went into their possession by which they, by communicating to newspapers could obtain large soma of money. Under such circumstances it was of the greatest importance that secrecy should be secured.— The vote was ultimately agreed to, and progress reported. RIVERS CONSERVANCY AND FLOODS P.,3I.RVATION BILL. —lt was agreed that Mr. Pugh and Mr. Arthur Balfour be added to the 19 members already named as a committee on this bill.—Mr. E. STaxitora moved that the committee be empowered to take evidence.—Mr. nonsore objected, as he thought such an arrangement would prevent the bill pass- ing this session.—Mr. Stanhope's motion was rejected by 116 against 63.—The Rivers' Floods Prevention Bill and petition for and against both were referred to the com- mittee.
The report of supply was received, and the sitting suspended.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S MARKETS.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S MARKETS.

LIVERPOOL COTTON, FRIDAY.—The market opens with a good inquiry and the sales are estimated at 10,000 bales, at steady prices. Futures firm. The only transaction so far is June- July at 6 15-64 d, which shows an advance of 1-64 d. The Ameri- can market for spottotton were steady yesterday at previous prices, with an advance of is at Mobile. Futures opened at a slight advance, then reacted, and closed at a decline of 2 to points for near, but an advance of Ito 2 for distant cotton. Bales 71,000 bales. Futures at New Orleans were 4 to 6 points lower. Bales 45,000 bales Receipts 4,400 bales, against 3,900 last week and 2,000 last year.

_ LIVERPOOL CORN, FRIDAY.—There was a good attendance at this morning's market, and wheat met with a better demand at an advance of ld per cental on Tuesday's prices. Flour quiet, but rices are steady Indian ern is without change, only • moderate business passing. Beans inactive, but previous prim; are maintained. Peas in only limited demand. Oats and meal iin fair request at unchanged values.

LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, PRIDAY.—Beef scarce and firmer. Pork quiet at the quotations. Prices for bacon rather irregu- lar. Hams sell better. Shoulders dull of sale Lard 3d to Id easier. Holders of cheese pressing sellers. Butter fiat.

div.head: EXPECTED RESIGNATION OF GAktEETTA.
div.p: EXPECTED RESIGNATION OF GAktEETTA.

- Paras, June 10.—Papers here generally admit a con`list between MM. Grevy and Gambetta has now commenced The proposition for a revision of the Constitution has no chance of acceptance by the Senate, and a general election is considered imminent on the question of revision and the abolition of the Senate put forth by Gambettiots. A stormy sitting of the Chamber to-morrow is anticipated. The pro- bability of M. Gambetta resigning the Presidency of the Chamber and resuming his old position as leader of the Par- liamentary majority is discussed in political circles. The Irreconcileable and Monarchist organs regard the Senate's vote as putting an end to M. Gambetta's dictatorship. Rumours are current this morning that M. Constans, M. Cazot, and General Farre, Ministers of the Interior, Justice, and War respectively, will tender their resignations, and it is also reported that M. Gambetta will resign the Presidency of the Chamber of Deputies.
INTERMENTS IN THE WARRINGTON CEMETERY. —Th• ' interments in the Warrington Cemetery for the week ending yesterday, were: Adults, 4; children, 9; total, 13.

LECTURE BY THE REV. J. A. BEET, ON THE NEW VERSIOIif —lt Will be Peen from our advertising columns that the Rev. J. A. Beet, of Warrington, will lecture on the "Revised New Testament," in Bethesda School, on Thursday evening next, under the auspices of the Runcorn Young Men'a Christian Association. Mr. Beet is well kne,wn in Theolo- gical circles as an able Greek and exegetical scholar, and, is therefore, well fitted to handle the subject he has chosen for his lecture, which will be specially interesting to Sunday school teachers. Mr. Beet "travelled" in the Runcorn circuit some years ago.

BANK PARK—The sylvan retreat of the inhabitants of Warrington, Bank Park, is now in its most attractive garb, and its beauties have been greatly enjoyed by the many persons who have nightly strolled through the grounds. The trees are resplendent with luxurious foliage, and both the park and gardens bear evidence of great care on the part of the gardeners, who have newly planted the Parterre, which at a later season present a sight of floral adornment that is generally greatly admired. At the present moment a charming aspect is imparted to the gardens by the rhodo- dendrons, which are in full bloom, and some excellent specimens are to be seen on the east side near the bee hives; while the hawthorn and other flowers emit a perfume most gratifying to, the senses. Another feature is the greenhouse well stocked with geraniums of variegated tints, and which will doubtless be the source of much attraction for some time to come.

Marsh, a salt dealer, by kicking him. in Turner-street Aboat six o'clock on Tuesday evening the prisoner went to the proscu- tor's house and commenced creating a disturbance. The prisoner was ordered away': but he knocked the prosecutor down, and, whilst he was on the ground, gave him .a violent kick in the mouth, splitting the lip, which had. to he sewn up. Later in the evening the prisoner again visited the house to create a disturbance, and he was lockr4 up by P.S. Berry. So far as we have been able to gather, the arrangements for Walking Day will be , similar to those of previous years. The schools connected with the Church of England will assemble at the Town Hall, at 10 a.m., and after being marshalled in their proper positions, will leave by the west gate and procession the principal streets on their way to the Parish Church. Divine service will commence at 11 o'clock, and the sermon will be preached by the Rev. M. Stevenson, clerical princi- pal of the Clergy Daughters' School, after which the scholars will return to the schools, where they will be dis, missed. The children will meet at their respective fields in the afternoon which will be given up to games, and other' recreations. I.Ce united demonstration will be made by the Nonconformist schools, who will ptoceed early in the morning, should the weather prove fine, direct to the ren- dezvous selected for the day's outing. According to custom the Roman Catholics will wend the day at one of the Popular sea-side resorts. The following day (Saturday) the employ& of various firms •4411 have their annual excur- sions, and as will he seen, from advertisements in another column, the wor'speople at Bank Quay Soap Works and Sankey Wire Mills intend going to Southport, the queen of Lancashire v,atering places, those employed at the Mersey and Latekford Tanneries aunouneing a trip to Blackpool.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY,

year, which you would have thought the Government would have made less than anything we had made, amounted to the sum of £134,505,000. (Applause.) Now that is an in- crease upon the expenditure of the year before of about a million and a half. Granted, for the sake of argument, they may say the same expenditure was necessary on the military and naval establishment. Ido not believe they will be able Ito reduce them next year in the least. I must refer to the 1 Queen's Speech once more. (A laugh.) It says that they want to amend the law of Ireland as regards the relations of landlord and tenant, and secondly, with the view of giving a larger proportion of the people by purchase a per.' manent proprietary interest in the soil. Now as to one of their propositions I have no objection at all, and that is to allowing the tenants to buy the land. If they choose to purchase well and good; but the way the Government are going to allow th2rn to purchase is p;oroc.. what curious. They are going to allow them tq borrow three-fourths of the purchase money from the State; and the other fourth from the usurer; and I do not see No— y a man can be said to buy a thing if he borrows three-fourths of the sum from the State, and the last fourth from a man who is sue to charge him an exorbitant interest. (Hear, hear.) I do not think that is a position that will give him much advantage, I think if helloes not pay the interest, and you are going to evict him, he will be apt to say that he is the owner of the place, and he will object to eviction just as much as the tenants object to eviction now. (Hear, hear.) I do not think by that means you will mend matters much; but if they had liked the process could have been carried on by the establishment of a land bank without the interven- tion of the State. (Hear' hear.) The other part of the Land Bill which I do object to is this: They say they are going to improve the relations of landlord and tenant. I quite approve of that if they can do so. But Ido not quite trust the man who is making the proposal—for two reasons. In the first place he tried his band at it in 1870 and entirely failed—(hear, hear)—and, in the next place, the propositions he now makes are diametrically opposed to those he then made, and no man in the House of Commons has ever made such an unanswerable argument against the proposals he makes now than the speeches he spoke in 1870. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) I object to the propositions on another ground, and it is this, because in my opinion they are giving a larger proportion of the people an interest by direct and absolute confiscation. • (Hear, hear, and cheers.) I will explain that in two words. They say that the ten- ant, by the action of the Land Bill of 1870, got something which he had not before, a sort of permanent interest in the soil which he can sell. Well, now, I have asked them over and over again, "What is it you can sell ? " Nobody has ever been able to tell us. We have asked, "Where is it to come from ?" There is only one place it can come from, and that is the landlord's pocket. (Hear, hear.) There are only two people engaged in the land—the landlord on the one side, and the tenant on the other; and if you give the tenant the power of selling something he has not now, the only place it can possibly come from is out of the land- lord's pocket. (Hear, hear.) I don't think I agree with the Duke of Areyll, that if you get the system it won't work well. But I put to you the plain question—if you are really going to take, as undoubtedly you are, money out of one man's pocket and put it into another's, ought you not to compensate him for doing so? That lathe whole question. Therefore, we say that this bill ;s absolute confiscation. If you are bound to take this course for the good of the State— we don't think this will do much good—if you do it, then you are bound to compensate the landlord for the loss he sustairs. (Hear, hear.) Only don't let the tenant think he is getting the whole advantage. I want to point out that although it may assist the actual individual tenant for the time, it is an absolute and positive wrong to all future tenants that ever may come hereafter. I cannot press that too strongly. If an incoming tenant was to take a farm, everybody knows he wants all the capital he can get for the purpose of tilling his farm. As matters are now, he has only to settle with his landlord to pay a fair and just rent. I have no objection whatever to rent being fair, and if you cannot make them so by agreement, then let it be done in some way. Bat the incoming tenant will have to riay the rent to the landlord; he will have to pay the outgoing tenant !for manure, improvements, and matters of that kind; but beyond that he will have to pay a premium, a goodwill for the right to go in—not to the landlord, but to the tenant. And all this will be a dead loss to him, and will hamper him during the whole time he is situated in that farm. Therefore, the point I want to press is this: This Bill is not for the good of the permanent tenants of Ireland. If it was I should be glad to listen to it. But it is for the benefit of the existing tenants, who only get it because the Government want to satisfy the clamour which has been made throughout the length and breadth of Ireland. (Hear, I hear.) Don't think that the way to govern—that by giving I up principles and departing from sound economic principles —you will settle any agitation in the world. What you want is that the authority of the Queen shall be vindicated, and that law and order shall be upheld. (Cheers.) The Government will find out that if there is to be a Govern- ment, it must govern. The Government will find out that, in order to be strong in action, it must be united in counsel. The Government will find out that the people of this country will not trust any body of people if they yield to the pres- sure, the outcry, the clamour of the mob, and depart from sound principles which everybody recognises as sound. (Applause.) A Government to receive the support of the people of this country must be firm as well as conciliatory, Just as well as generous; and I venture to say of this Government, that no Government has ever made so many mistakes and blunders of so serious a character in so short a time—(loud applause)—and whenever it comes before the ' bar of public opinion, unless it changes very much from the course which it has been pursuing, I, for one, have not the smallest doubt or hesitation as to the verdict, not which you in Lancashire alone will give' but which will be given throughout the length and breadth of this country. (Loud cheers, amidst which the right hon. gentleman resumed his seat). Lieutenant Colonel J. IRELAND BLACKBURNF, M.P., who was heartily received, said :—After the able and exhaustive speech to which we have had the pleasure of listening, I shall not long engage your attention ; but it will be neces- sary for me to say a few words on this great occasion. (Cheers.) When I remember the last time I had the honour of being in this room and witnessing the magnificent re- ception which you gave us, and when I remember the great demonstration you made on the day of election—(cheers)— and now see the reception you give us on the first occasion on which we are able to come among you, I cannot but be deeply. sensible of the honour you have conferred upon me, in conjunction with my right hon. colleague. (Loud cheers.) Sir Richard Cross has gone through a great variety of sub- jects connected with the policy of the present Government, which has been marked by arrogance, blunders, and un- fulfilled promises, the most striking, in my opinion, being in regard to the government of Ireland. (Hear, hear.) Who can remember without extreme horror the action of the Executive during the last autumn? If they had acted effi- ciently, if the law had been insisted upon, we should not now have been lamenting the horrors which are now occur- ring and the increasing anxiety which they are causing as to the future, (Hew, heart awl cheers.? Although they had lost their chief, they The soldiers had returned to Skibbereen. were not so badly off as the Radicals, as it would be difficult A Cork correspondent •reports that the railway line to tell who would be leader if Mr. Gladstone had to go. between Skibbereen and Bandon was torn up on Wednesday They had gone through the tire, and they need not despair at a point called Mutton Bridge, within a mile of Drimo- so long as they had Lord Salisbury, Lord Richmond, Lord league. The object of the outrage was to intercept a train Cairns in the House of Lords, and Sir Stafford Northcote, which was returning with about 100 men of the Rifle Sir R. Cross, and Colonel Blackburn, and men of their stamp Brigade, who proceeded to Skibbereen on Tuesday night. in the House of Commons. (Cheers.) Fortunately the driver of the train saw the danger in time The members were then escorted to the railway station to draw up. The road was repaired, and the train arrived amid the cheers of their supporters. in Cork after a delay of an boor and a half. Fifty police- men havegonedown the line by the return train. A telegram received on Wedneseay says :—Authentic information of the doings in West Cork have at last reached Cork. Father Murphy was not in the first place arrested, though some busybody spread the intelligence that he was. ANOTHER MILITARY FIASCO. A correspondent, writing from Limerick on Wednesday nitzlit, says that the employment of a large body of troops and constabulary at GIM, at the mouth of the Shannon, had no practical result. A special train left Limerick station with sixty infantry of the Ist and 9th Regiments, and thirty cavalry of the 20th Hnssars, with three ambulance waggons; and about thirty constables were sent to Foynes overnight, and the entire constabulary force which assembled at Fortes in the morning amounted to over one hundred. The cavalry and a portion of the infantry proceeded to Glin by road, and the rest were taken on board her Majesty's gunboat Bruiser at Odin. A column was formed, which marched through the village toward the Ballygiltmane estate, on which it was intended to seize cattle in satisfaction of an annuity of £3OO a year charged on the estate under a marriage settlement. Mrs. Groggan, the annuitant, accompanied the expedition, but though the utmost seereey had been observed with regard to the object all the cattle had been removed from off the respective tenements, and there was nothing to seize. The appearance of the troops in force caused much excitement, but there was no collision between the representatives of authority and the people. The estate on which the seizures were attempted te be made is nearly 1,000 acres, principally of mountain land, valued in the aggregate by Griffiths at £BO, bat let at over £360. THE RIOTING AT CLONMEL. Six persons were sent for trial to Clonmel Quarter Ses- sions by the Tipperary magistrates on Wednesday, for being concerned in disturbances and burning of a caretaker's but, erected by the Property Defence Society, at Banslea 01a deserted farm belonging to Mrs. Elizabeth Roe, of Dublin. The police, who interfered to protect the workmen were stoned. The Riot Act was read, and the mob was charged. A considerable detachment of the Guards are under orders at Dublin for the south, and will be despatched this morning. Their exact destination is, however, not known. Powell, the tenant farmer whose ears were recently clipped at Glenbagh, county Kerry, has taken refuge in the police barracks, his life having been threatened. The police in the district have been reinforced.

The monthly meetiug of this Board, called for Tuesday, could not be held owing to there not being a sufficient num- ber of members present to form a quorum. The only memberf present were Mr. W. L. Evans, J.P., the chairman, and Mr. It. Tyrer. SURVEYOR'S EXPENDITURE. The Surveyor (Mr. W. Goldsworth) submitted his state- ment of expenditure for the month of May, from which it appeared that he had expended in connection with the township of Bold, the sum of £l2 103; Knowsley, £33 17s 4d; Rainhill, £ll Os 6d; Whiston, £lO 5s ; team labour, 00 7s 6d; new materials, £5B 13s 4d; incidental expenses £2 53 8d; total, £2OB 19s 4d.

FINANCB. It was stated that the amount owing ta the treasurer was £l5O 2s 3d. Since the last meeting the overseers of ton and and Knowsley had paid £2OO and £lOO respectively on account of the calls made ypon them. The amount still owing by the various townships comprising the Board's dis- trict was £75, as follows:—Bold, £150; Knowsley, £225 ; Rainhill, £300; and Whiston, £2oo.—The Clerk was in- structed to write to the overseers of the several townships urging immediate payment.

HUTTON V. NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS.—The first match thi season between the first elevens of these clubs took place on Saturday last, at Huyton, and resulted in a decided victory for the home team by three wickets and 67 runs. The wicket was in splendid condition, thanks to W. Marriott, the energetic professional of the club, and the weather being fine there was a fair attendance of spectators, including a sprinkling of the fair sex. The visitors were the first to assume the defensive, the opening of the score being entrusted to 0. Emmett and J. Pen- nington. Rigby and Reichardt were entrusted with the ball. After a single, Rigby found his way to Emmett's wicket, and the vacancy was filled by E. Fairclough. After some hard hit- ting Pennington knocked the ball into the bowler's hands, and he was succeeded by T. Slater, and G, Tonsey having relieved Reichardt at the pavilion end of the wicket, play was again commenced. Two more runs having been added to the score, which now stood at 26, the new bowler separated Fakelough's wickets. J. Fairclough was next man, but he met with a like fate, and his place was filled by J. Ball, an old cricketer. Runs now came pretty freely, and at 46 a change with the bowling was made, Bretherton taking the place of Tonsey, and the latter the place of Rigby. At 53 Ball was bowled off his leg, and the next three batsmen were disposed of without covering a single run, one of them (Dudgeon) being admirably stumped by. B. Tackaon. F. Fairclongh then joined Slater, but a separation was soon effected, the latter, who had seen five of his brethren fall, being bowled by Bretherton for 15.. Another change in the bowling was made at 77, Reichardt being substituted in Place of Tonsey, and a couple of runs having been added, the last corner-in returned the ball to the bowler, and the innings closed for a total of 79. After the usual interval the home team went to the wickets, J. W. Graham and R. Rigby being the fire'. representatives. Before double figures had been got into. Graham was bowled by Slater, and the wickets of the new corner, F. Jowett, came to grief in the same over of the same trundler. W. Gorst then became Rigby's vis-a-vis, but after making seven he was taken at mid-off, and was followed by E. Jackson, the score standing at 23 for three wickets. The new corner opened his account by driving Fairclough for three, and as-the runs came rather too quickly for the captain of the visit- ing team, he changed the bowling at 29, Ball taking the place of Fairclough. Half a century having been telegraphed, the underhand bowler secured Jackson's wickets with a "hopper." Rigby was then partnered by W. Wainwright, and Emmett took the ball from Slater. The score having been supple- mented by a couple, Rigby was disposed of by the new bowler, and the gap was filled by G. Jowett. The score was now 52, and, despite the repeated changes in the bowling, the runs came so rapidly that the visitors' score of 79 was soon wiped off, both Wainwright and Jowett "laying" into the bowling right merrily, especially the former, who made some capital drives, including a four off Slater and nine three's. Before a separation took place the telegraph board showed 128, when Jowett lost his wicket, after putting together the appreciable score of 26, which included four three's, three two's, and singles. C. Aldrich was next man, but his partner immediately after succumbed to the bowling of Fairclough, after a well played Innings of 50 without a single chance. The in-batsman was then faced by 0 Reichardt, and the two played out time, the score standing at 146 for seven- wickets. The following is the score:—

Florence, the beautiful! was before us for a rapid survey, as we turned out of our hotel by the side of the Arno next morning at 8 am. Having left each other perfectly free until breakfast, Mr. Nimmo and I passed across the bridge, e, Alla Carraia," and soon found ourselves within the Church of the Carmine. The way to it is through narrow streets. ' As usual on the Continent the shops were all open; no sus- pension of traffic or labour marking the Lord's day. The entrance into the church was through a dingy screen, with- in a plain unpretending doorway. Within its precincts is the celebrated Brancacci Chapel, which was saved from des- truction in 1771 when the rest of the building was destroyed by fire. In this chapel are twelve of the finest paintings in Italy, nine of which were painted in the 15th c_e_tttill.by Masaccio, who died at twenty-nine years of age. atm guide book says: "The greatest artists the world has produced have studied before these paintings, such as Leonareli de Vinci, Raphael, Audrea del Sarto, and Michael Angelo." In all paintings and interior .d.eceoravtalovnids obfletnhids. fine old place there is a subdued, but eaglets'tiv . ing of colours, which almost lifts one out of himself with admiration. We visited two other far more celebrated places during the day, "Santa Croce," and" Santissima viz, Annunziata," but neither of these pleased me so much in the general effect, as the Chnrch of the Carmine. Yet, what a plain, almost dirty-looking building it is outside. inethintgo you cannot but•notice with approbation, as appertaining all the churches on the Continent, as it does to all the Mosquess in the East, and that is the perfect freedom with which all classes find their way into them. Here were servant girls coming, in their kitchen garb and without bonnets, to pay their early morning devotioos, finding ne hindrance either in their own pride or the pride of others. Only think of such finding their way into the seats of our purse-proud pew proprietors in England! What a stiffen- ing of the neck and a curling of the lip there would be! Verger ! door-keeper! Why don't you turn this person out ?" We noticed that in Florence the men worshippers were much more numerous than in Paris. Having but one day for Florence, and wishing to take the opportunity afforded by the day of seeing the churches and their worship to the greatest advantage, we procured a guide after breakfast, and sallied forth under his leading. Guides who undertake to chaperon Englishmen or Englishwomen are usually under- stood to speak a little English. Well, ours did speak a little, but it was eery little, and that little, I must say, was very often" Dutch" to us! Beautiful, wonderfully beauti- ful as Forence is, seen from an eminence; rich an she is in magnificent public buildings, and in works of art, the general aspect of the streets disappointed US. Instead of open squares and wide airy thoroughfares, ornamented and shaded with long rows of trees, nothing but the high and heavy walls of her grey and massive houses met the eye, the thick iron bars on nearly all the windows adding no lo to the frown with which they seemed to look down upon us. On our way to the Church of S. Annunziata we dropped into the Cburch of San Giovanni, an octagonal temple, in which are performed most of the baptisms in Florence. It is celebrated for its magnificent bronze doors of the 14th and 15th centuries, one of which is considered so beautiful and perfect that even Michael Angelo said it was worthy to be the door of Paradise. It is also celebrated for its vaulted roof of Roman Mosaics of the 13th century, re- presenting the " Last Judgment." On entering, we found the priests just concluding the christening of a babe. After a considerable time had been occupied in registering and re- ceiving the fees, another was brought forward, when the aged officiating priest, attended by his junior, came down from the baptistery into the body of the church, where the yet unconsecrated child was held by a handsome, blushing young fellow, who evidently felt, in thisfirst attempt to hold a baby, that all eyes were fixed upon him. The sweet demure looking mother stood by his side, while the elder priest gabbled over the baptismal service as fast as his tongue could go ; and his junior shot out of his lips at the prescribed places "Amen !" This performance ended, the parents and the places, were led up to the font, where the aged priest, still rapidly talking, touched the eyes, ears, and mouth of the babe. The poor little thing being swathed, and thereby made as stiff as a wooden doll, was now held up by the father, as if to receive the charge, and to receive it with attention. Then its head was bowed down over the font, while the priest, with his silver basin, poured the water two or three times pretty profusely over it. Here I expected a scream, but probably the water had been warmed, as the babe failed to "give mouth" at this point, although it had been protesting rather vehemently before. In gazing upon the wonders of art so profusely lavished, both externally and internally, on the charches with which Florence abounds, of course one's eyes were dazzled—one's love of the beautiful completely satiated but the soul was far from being spiritualised or satisfied. Why, then, should I further dwell on those things, which, though costly in production beyond all cal- culation, and artistically perfect, it may be, beyond all pre- vious things of the kind, have so trifling and ephemeral an interest in comparison with those which affect the moral nature and prospects of mankind? I therefore pass by the merely external to notice the character of the worship, and, to some extent, its influence upon the people. The first thing that struck me was the freeness with which, led by our guide, we, and all other mere sight-seers, were allowed, indeed encouraged, to thread our way among the worship- pers, coming between them in their worship and their 4 favourite altars, scarcely any matter how near they might e be kneeling. It should be noted that certain chapels and • confessionals within these large churches are dedicated to certain saints; and the worshippers have to make choice which of the saints they will employ to secure for them absolution in the court of heaven. Another thing we noticed was the nearness with which even the poorest of the people were permitted to approach to the officiating priests as they ministered at the chief altar, standing on the step, lining the way right up to the table on • which mass was being performed. Although this fervour of religious feeling remains with a few I am of opinion that the Romish system in these old cities is fast waning to decay. In one of the side chapels a priest was conducting the service. As far as he himself was con- cerned, the service was conducted with due amount of de- • corum and formality; but alongside of him a dirty looking I boy was leaning upon the altar with his elbow, uttering the responses. This was done parrot-like all the while the urchin was looking about him, and taking in all that was passing. Before paseing out of the precincts of this grand old struc- ture, we should remember that some of the earth's greatest and most admired artists, poets, philosophers, and statesmen rest beneath its dome "Here repose Angelo's Allen's bones, and his The starry Galileo, with his woes. Here Machiavellis, each returned to whence it rose." Facing the church in the spacious square, is one of the finest statues in the world. It was raised in honour of the poet Dante, in 1865, on the occasion of the rejoicing for the sixth centennial of his birth, and the translation of the capital of Italy from Turin to Florence. A more spiritualised piece of marble I never saw! There the poet stands, with face up- lifted, and with eye transfixed, gazing in rapt contemplation, until you feel that it would be no surprise if the statue, "impregnated with divinity," were to leave its lofty pedes- tal and soar into the sky. In raising this noble and brilliant work of art to the honour of her great poet, Florence has amply responded to the challenge of Lord Byron, and, speak- ing after the manner of men, rolled away a long-standing reproach. Byron asks : " And has his country's marbles nought to say? Could not her quarries furnish forth one bust?' Here it is! breathing with immortality! in poetic style. As we went into a restaurant a very pretty damsel, dressed with extreme taste and neatness, was just coming out. We had scarcely taken our seats when she returned, and after present- ing each of us with a flower, went into an adjoining room. Supposing she belonged to the house, and that tins was a Florentine welcome, we felt gratified that, even in these lower rills of life, the love of the beautiful, for which Florence is so famed, should find so sweet and fragrant an expression. To so handsome and ladylike a person we never dreamt of offering a few ttous in payment. It was very stupid, for why should not the beautiful in Florence extend to the ensemble of her flower-girls as to all other things? And why should not flower-girls be paid for their flowers? Having accepted the flowers, we, of course, were not slow to accept this view of the case when it was put before us, and on her re-appearance in the room were pre- pared, with the assistance of our guide, to see that she de- parted with as many smiles and with as much grace as she had presented the flowers. Florence was on the eve of the carnival. Great excitement reigned in the streets; the men strode about in their graceful cloaks and slouch hate; and the women, beautiful almost to perfection, dressed, too, with exceeding taste, passed to and fro in equal numbers. Anything like a vulgar or tawdry mixing of colours are scarcely to be seen. But by the side of all this elegance and grace there was a social element very depress- ing to the thoughtful onlooker. I refer to the extremely poverty-stricken appearance of the peasant population. Into this city of marble palaces and costly ecclesiastical edifices the poor tillers of the soil were bringing there few • vegetables on carts that would scarcely stick together. I do not think I saw a good cart in Florence—one better than our ragmen in England would be ashamed to own. Before closing my account of Florence I must note our ride by a very delightful winding road, which presented many beauti- ful views of the city, to Piazzali Michael Angelo, a vast and splendid square, situated high above the level of the city, and from which the finest view of it is obtained. On this elevated plateau we stood for several minutes in wondering admiration at the exceeding beauty of the panorama. As we left the hill our guide drew our attention to an avenue of cyprus trees, a mile long, which had a very noble and pleasing effect. (To be continued next meek.)

LANCASISIIIIS Younentaws.— / considerable number of Volunteer encampments were formed on the coast on Satur- day. The Ist M.R.V. are under canvas at Lytham; the 2nd have gone to Colwyn Bay. Regiments from other Lanca- shire towns are encamped along the coast at Southport and Blackpool. The annual prize meeting of the Lancashire Rifle ABSOCiatiOFI was commenced on Saturday at Altcar. Lie number of entries for all the competitions was over 1,600, being slightly in excess of the number last year.

RITIsiCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit (chairman) Ind mt. Henry Reynolds. SEEIOES WIFE ASSAIILT.—FeIix Me,Conn, a delapidated- looking man, Was charged with assaulting his wife Cather- ine, on the 4th inst.—P.C. gossons and Inspector Holling- worth gave evidence to the effect that the defendant, who is much addicted to drinking, was found by them on Satur- day night in Back Mersey-street, throttling and kicking his wife. Her face was in a terrible condition.—Defendant said his wife asked him for money to drink, and on his re- fusing to give it her she set upon him, and he had to hold her down to prevent her doing mischief.—Defendant was I fined 20s. and costs Ss. 4d., or in default of payment one month's imprisonment. Manama, recvr MATED.—Alfred Bentley, a weigher em- ployed at Weston Chemical Works, was charged with assaulting his wife on the 26th ult.—Complainant said defendant came home drunk at night, pulled her hair, and kicked her.—Complainant,who isgifted with an exceedingly fluent tongue, had to be called to order several times by the Bench.—Defendant said that what with his wife and his mother-in-law he led a sorry life. On the least dispute be- tween them, his wife ran home to her mother to tell her everything.—The Chairman said it was quite evident the wife had a sharp temper; and it would, perhaps, be as well if they were to come to an agreement to separate. As there was no corroborative evidence the case would be dismissed. PERMISSION TO Snw..—The following permissions to sell until next transfer day, were granted: The Navigation Inn, from Henry Jackson to Thomas Walker; the Castle Hotel, Halton, from Berthold Rehberg to Win. Phillips; add Wil- son's Hotel, from James Knowles to Henry Jackson. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. James Reynolds. A Roman CESTOMER.—Peter Cadbury was summoned for causing a breach of the peace in High-street on the previous night. He was also charged with assaulting P.C. JamesW. Baker whilst in the execution of his duty ; and Thomas Loughlan and Patrick Russell were charged with resisting the officer. The evidence showed that Cadbury was fighting with another man in High-street, and Baker, who was in plain clothes, went up, telling him that he was a police officer, and he must stop such conduct. Cadbury refused, on which the officer tried to prevent him, and received two violent blows in the face. He then took the fellow into custody, ou which the two other defendants said he should not take Cadbury to the police station, and did all they could to prevent him.—The magistrates ordered Cadbury to be bound over for fighting, in his own recognizances of Z, to keep the peace six months, and he and the two other de- fendants had each 10s. and costs to pay for resisting the

police. Ygsruntray.—Before Mr. Wm. Bankes. ALLEGED SAVAGE ASSAULT ON A DITTGN MAN BY TWO lEISHMEN.—Dorninic Coleman and Patrick Coleman, two powerful-looking men, Irishmen, were charged with unlaw- fully wounding Thomas Hughes.—The complainant stated that he lived at Ditton, and on Whit-Monday, between six and seven o'clock, having been at Halton, he was returning by the usual walk, on one side of which was a wall about five feet high and on the other an embankment. On meet- ing with the two defendants and another man who accom- panied them, without a word passing between them, the prisoner Dominic Coleman threv his foot out before him and knocked him down. One of the men said he was an English --, and Patrick Coleman kicked him on the front part of the head, causing him to bleed very much. He was afterwards kicked a number of times, and begged them, for God's sake, not to kill him. Prisoners then ran off up the fields. About five minutes afterwards, P. C. Lowndes came up, saw the pool of blood, and he told him how he had been assaulted. When the complainant had given part of his evidence, Mr. Beasley said he had aa objection to raise, on the part of the prisoners, against the case being proceeded with. He submitted that the prisoners had settled the case with the complainant, and, this being so, there was an end of the matter.—Mr. Bankes: That is a question for the Bench.—Mr. Beasley said the injury was a private one which might be settled by the parties amongst themselves, if they choose. If complainant had thought it, he might have entered a complaint in the County Court, and sued for damages, but instead of this, he had agreed with the friends of the prisoners to settle the case without the intervention of the court.—Mr. Johnson, deputy magistrates' clerk: .Does that do away with the jurisdiction of the magistrate —Mr. Beasley: I say it does.—Mr. Johnson: The corn- plainant cannot even setle a common assault out of court, much more a case of unlawfully wounding.—Mr. Beasley submitted on the highest authority, that it was quite com- petent for complainant to settle the matter. He quoted from "Stone's Manual," the case of Fisher against the Apollinaris Company, in which the Lords Justices held that even where there had been a committal for trial, the indictment might be lawfully compromised. Their lordships applied this dictum generally to cases in which a party had his remedy in a civil court. He also maintained that the prisoners were not properly in custody, as the officer who took then/ in charge had not seen the assault committed.—Mr. Bankes: The case must go on; I shall not allow it to be withdrawn.—Mr. Beasley; I am surprised to hear you come to that decision, even if it be on the advice of the Deputy Magistrates' Clerk.—Mr. Bankes: That is my decision.—The evidence was then proceeded with. Dr. McDougall said the complainant had bled pro- fusely before arriving at his surgery. His face was covered witlashlood. On examining him, ha found a wound 11 in. in length on the front part of the head, and the skin and tissue underneath were cut to the bone. The wound was such as would be caused by direct violence.—ln cross- examination, complainant said the prisoners were about half drunk. Witness had had " middling " himself. It was true that since the assault he had entered into an arrangement with the friends of the prisoners not to bring the case before the magistrates.—P.C. Lowndes gave evidence as to being called to Halton village on the evening of the assault, owing to some Irishmen making a disturbance. On the way he met Hughes who told him about the prisoners having assaulted him. He went after the men, when Hughes gave them in charge. In reply to complainant, the pri- soners said, "I think you are wrong." Whilst going through the fields, on the way to the Runcorn police station, the prisoner Dominic. Coleman tried to make his escape, and succeeded in getting aFross two fields, but he was stopped I by a man. At the polioe station the prisoners were charged 1 With unlawfully wounding. Patrick said, "Yes," and the other prisoner made no reply.—Mr. Beasley said he was willing to admit that the prisoner Patrick Coleman did as- sault the complainant, but it Was owing to his using offen- sive remarks to him as he was pasaing through the fields. He submitted that the offence might be dealt with as a com- mon assault.—A farm labourer named Michael Coleman said he worked at Rock Savage, and at the time of the alleged assault he was with the prisoners, when they met complainant and another man. Complainant told the pri- soners to go to —, and then Patrick followed him, but Dominic did not go near him.—Mr. Bankes said the assault was a most gross and unwarrantable one, and the prisoner Dominic Coleman bad been previously convicted of unlaw- fully wounding. Each of the prisoners would be committed to knutsford Quarter Sessions for trial, and bail would be refused.

The officers had, however, been unable to find any of the money, or to obtain any further evidence in the case. Though there was a strong suspicion that the prisoners had had something to do with the robbery, yet as he was unable to offer suffi- cient evidence to enable him to ask the magistrates to commit the prisoners for trial, he must ask for their, dis- charge. The women, who took the matter very coolly, were then set at liberty. A DEAR LOT OF BAD MUSSELS : £4 Ts. 6d. TO PAT.— John Barton, fish-dealer, Wellington-street, was summoned by the Widnes Local Board, who were represented by their Clerk, for exposing for sale 432 mussels, on the 14th April, which were afterwards ordered to be destroyed by Mr. George Pilkington, magistrate.:—Mr. Beasley said the defendant was charged under the section which rendered a dealer liable to a fine not exceeding £2O, for every piece of bad fish exposed for sale, or the magistrates had a i discretionary power to in- flict a sentence of three months' imprisonment. The Beard's officers bad had a good deal of trouble with the defendant at times, and had frequently overlooked what had been sus- picious conduct on his part.—Mr. Sheppard, superintendent of the market, and assis'ant inspector of nuisances, said he was passing the defendant's shop about ten o'clock in the morning, and found it partly closed (the door merely being open). He noticed the mussels on the footpath in front of i the shop, and defendant's lad n charge of them. They were in a basket, and, on enquiring thg price, he found it to be one penny a quart. He asked to see defendant, but was told he was away, and it was not known when he would re- turn. He then seized the mussels, and called the attention of Mr. Dickson, nuisance inspector, to them. They were taken before Mr. George Pilkington, J.l',. who ordered them to be destroyed. The reason why the case had not been brought before the Bench at an earlier day, was that witness had been seriously ill, and therefore unable to attend court. —Mr. John Dickson gave corr borative evidence as to the mussels being unfit for food.—A stonemason, named John Drummond, of Wellington-street, was called by defendant for the purpose of saying that he heard Barton tell his lad to throw Ike fish into the ash place, but it appeared he had neglected to do so after his father had gone away by train. On tile night of the same day as they were seized, defendant saw him and told him his boy kid not followed out his in- structions, and that the Local Board's officials intended "to make a case of it." CATHOLIC SCHOOL LADS TRESPASSING. - Thomas Calleghan a youth, had 7s. 6d. costs to pay for trespassing on grass belonging to Mr. Water Longton, on the 7th inst. —Complainant said that the boy was accompanied by about ten others, who had jast come out of the Catholic schools. AN ALLEGED SEDUCER AND HIS CREOLE VICTIEL.— A sorrowful-looking young woman of interesting appearance, who it was stated was a Creole named Mary Fernandez, was brought up under peculiar circumstances.--The Inspector of Police stated that about a fortnight ago the defendant tried to take away her life by drinking oxalic acid. She after- wards became very ill, and had only just recovered suffi- ciently to attea4 court. He understood that the poor girl was a domestic servant out of place, and she had surrendered that morning to the charge of attempting to commit suicide. She had expressed her sorrow for trying to take her life, and there was no desire to press the ease on the part of the police.—A kind-hearted woman who had taken the defen- dant to her home, and acted the part of a good Samaritan to her, said that she had been betrayed by her lover, and was now with cbild.—Mr. Lewin, deputy magistrates' clerk, said he hoped defendant would come to a determination not to kill herself for the sake of any man. He also advised her to take out a summons for the purpose of proving the paternity of the child as soon as it was born.—The Bench discharged (he prisoner, on the woman promising to take . defendant into her care, until some way wts sten out of her , present troubles.

The usual camp meetings, which have proved so popular in previous years, were held on Runcorn Hill, by the Primitive Methodists. The members of the Salvation Army were found, to use the words of one of their popular tunes, to be "marching along." They issued special placards stating that their meetings would be addressed by the Black Prince, a somewhat corpulent York- ishireman, who, we understand, obtained this title not, as many might suppose, from his skin being black, but owing to his being at one time a prince in wickedness—one of those written about in so interesting a manner by rare John Bunyan, in the "Holy War." Happy Charley and a number of "Salvation prophetesses" also favoured the gatherings with addresses. THE TRIENDLY SOCIETIES. ' •

' This is a great day for visitors to Overton, Frodsham, and Helsby, and thousands left the town for these favourite resorts, so that throughout the day the Runcorn Station presented a very crowded appearance. We regretted to see that the number of visitors to the town who gave themselves up to the intemperate worship of Old John Barleycorn was so numerous. Indeed, at one part of the evening, a foot pas- senger could not go above thirty yards in the principal streets without meeting with some poor fellow under the in- fluence of drink. It is somewhat remarkable that when times are said to be so bad and work so scarce men should be such simpletons as te spend their little all in swallowing an excessive quantity of that which steals away their brains. The writer is not an abstainer, but as one having a little patriotism in his soul he wonders what a foreigner must think when he sees so many drunken fellows in our streets. The temperance sccieties have a great work bide before they make English workingmen as sober and careful as our neigh- bours across the channel.
