div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday, at the Cemetery, Mr. Thomas Norman presided, and there were also present Messrs. Coleburn, Littler, and Salkeld (sec.) The business was mostly of a formal character. The Secre- tary read the monthly returns, which showed the interments to have been 23, of whom nine were Churchmen, 12 Dissenters, and two Roman Catholics. The total number of interments up to May 25th were 5,471, of whom 2,223 were Churchmen, 2,790 Dissenters, and 452 Catholics. On the Ist inst., a person named Charles Lawson, of Weston, was buried in the unconsecrated portion of the ground by the Rev. J. J. Bryant, clergyman. Accounts amounting to £l7 113 s. were passed for payment, and £37 ss. 10d. due for iaterest. The Board signed the usual notice to the over- seers to call a vestry meeting on the 30th inst., for the pur- pose of appointing three ratepayers as members of the Burial Board, in the place of Messrs. Thomas Nerman, lames Handley, and George Marshall, who go out of office by rotation, but are eligible for re-appointment. It was stated that the sum of £l2O had been received from the overseers; and also £lOO from the Grand United Order of Oddfeliows, on mortgage, at 4 per cent interest. The Secretary informed the Board that the receipts for the month were £l5 Os. 61, acd the payments £9l3s. 3d., leavings balance of £5 7s. 3d At the close of the business, the members visited the new mortuary, and, on the motion of Mr. Coleburn, seconded by Mr. Littler, it was resolved that the west room of the building should be used exclusively as a mortuary, and that the second room should be set apart for the dead bodies of those who had died from an infectious disease.

_ NEWTON AND EARL ESTOWN. NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS. Mr. Gooch, chairman, presided at the monthly meet- ing held at the Newton Town Hall, on Tuesday (in conse- quence of Monday being Whit Monday). There were also present Messrs. Winstonley, Woods, Pardey, Foster, J. E. Woreley (law clerk) and R. Brierley (surveyor). THE COMMISSIONERS AND THE ALKALI BILL. The LAW CLERK: I received a print from one of the mem- bers of Parliament I had seen as to the Alkali Bill as to the objections and amendments which had been given notice of, and I see the amendment which the Commissioners proposed, and sent me up to London to see the members of Parliament about, has been adopted by Mr. Dodson, and was moved by him.—The CHAIRMAN: Oh, that is satisfactory.—Mr. WIN- STANLEY: Our Law Clerk will be quite a public benefactor 500n.—The Law CLERK: Why ?—Mr. WINSTANLEY: By such wise suggestions that are adopted for the benefit of the pnblic.—The Law CLERK: Mr. Dodson has adopted them, so that I think they will have a good chance of being earned onto, - HIGHWAYS, PUBLIC WORKS, AND SANITARY COMMITTEE. At a meeting of this committee, the Surveyor had reported that Mr. Pardey would not agree that Mr. Legh should covenant with his lessees to sewer Vista Road when called upon by the Commissioners. The committee recommended that the road be not repaired and adopted by the township unless Mr. Pardey gives an authority to that effect, and also for the flagging of the footpaths.—lt was ordered that the occupier of Park Side quarry be called upon to fence the same along Park Side road. Plans for a house and shop in Oxford-street, for Mr. John Lambert, two houses in Market street, for Mr. George Proffitt, lodge in Church-street, for Mr. arlcCorquodale, Rad a cottage in High-street, for Mr. A. Cart- wright, were submitted and approved.—Mr. Woon moved the confirmation of the minutes.—Mr. WiNsTANLny seconded the motion, and remarked that the quarry at Park Side was in a most dangerous state, and it was absolutely necessary it should be fenced. After some conversation Mr. PARDEY, referring to the minute relating to Vista-road, said he thought when the committee sat they could hardly under- stand the exact situation. The new road was made in sub- stitution of a very old township read. Before the road was made the consent of the Haydock Highway Board and the Newton Commissioners was obtained, and inasmuch as the old road bad no sewer whatever he did not think it would be either just or equitable to ask Mr. Lea to put a sewer in the new road.—Mr. WINSTANLEY could not see what hardship it would be to the people who leased the land to put in a sewer.—Mr. PARDEY said that would be right enough if the rule were applied throughout the township. In every other public road the sewer was paid for out of the public purse.—Ultimately, the minutes were referred back to the committee. THE BURIAL GROUND QUESTION. A special meeting of the Highways &c. Committee was held, at which the committee considered it advisable that steps should be at once taken for providing a public burial grsund for the district, and that a site of about 10 acres, situate between Park-road and New Hey Farm, east of Green Main's Pits, be recommended as suitable for the pur- pose—The minute was confirmed on the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. PARDEY. THE CONSUMPTION OF GAS AND WATER. The Gas and Water Committee held a meeting on the 16th ult., when Mr. Brierley reported that the make of gas for the year ending March, 1881. was 19,935,100 cubic feet —consumed by meter 10,575,200 feet, by lamps and works 1,200,000 feet, unaccountable and leakages 2,159,900 feet. The consumption of water for the year amounted to 28,555,900 gallons, or about 83,000 gallons per day. It was ordered that quotations be invited for the supply of gas coals for two or three years, and that Mr. .Brierley arrange for a trial of the fire apparatus.—l he minutes were adopted. THE RATES.—REDUCTION IN THE PRICE OF OAS. A meeting of the Finance Committee was held on the 16th May, when accounts amounting to £353 2s. sd. were examined, and cheques signed for payment. At a meeting held on the 7th inst., the estimates for the rates were minutely examined, and it was agreed to recommend a high- way rate of Bd., a general district rate of 6d., a water rate of ltd., and a gas rate of Bd. in the Z. The committee re- commended the transfer of £2O, from the gas fund account to general improvement account, and also that the price of gas be redeced to 2s. od. per thousand feet nett to all con- sumers uniformly.—On the motion of Mr. WOOD, seconded Mr. PARDEY, the minutes were passed.

MACHINERY ACCIDENT AT EARLISTOWN VIIIYOCT WAGON WORIS.—On Thursday evening a boy named John Birks, employed at a cutting machine in the spring department of these works, whilst engaged cleaning the machine a few minutes before leaving off work, was suddenly caught by the right arm. The poor lad was promptly helped, but when extricated his arm was smashed right up to the muscles below the shoulder. Medical aid was at once sent for, but as no doctor could be found, Mr. Peake, chemist, bound up the remaining portionof the arm, and the lad was carefully carried on a stretcher to the station by four men, and conveyed by train to Liverpool. Ile now lies in a critical state in the Liverpool Infirmary, amputation having been performed at the shoulder. ENTEETAINMEN'Y AT ELELESTOWN.-011 Thursday even- ing an entertamment under the heading of "Be merry and wise," was given in the Earlestown Infant's School,in aid of St. John's church choir fund. The principal attraction was Professor Weeber, who dexterously and humourously went through some enjoyable " Wiaardism, and ventriloquism," to the gratification of the audience. The programme was made up by two comic dialogues, the first entitled "The three graces," was well sustained by Messrs. H. J. Durman, H. Waywell, R. Harrison, and W. Wills. "The wife hunters," was cleverly carried out by the Brothers Way- I well and T. Singleton.

FRODSITAM. LIM:MAL ASSOCIATION FOR FIZODSHAIL—A meeting of the Liberal electors of the Frodsham palling district in the West Cheshire division, was held in the Town Hall, Prod- bharn, on Saturday evening. Mr. Charles Reynolds, J.P., presided, and there was a good representative meeting from the several townships in the district. Mr. Jas. Tomkinson, of Willington Hall, who recentiv contested West Cheshire, attended, and explained the objects of the General Liberal Committee, and pointel out the necessity for the organisa- tion of t'm Liberal party and revision of the voters' lists. Resolutions were passed constituting those present a Liberal Association, and three delegates vrere7appointed to attend the general meeting to be held at Chester. The considera- tion of the new register was referred to a number of active local Liberals, and the meeting was brought to a close by a vote of thanks to the chairman.

THU CHEMICAL TRADE OF ST. HELENS.—Vie under- stand there is an improvement in the chemical trade of this town, and also in the chemical trade generally. For some time the trade, as has been the case with nearly all branches of industry, has not been as brisk as those engaged in it could have wished. The trade has not been steady, hate- - missions of dullness. being frequent. There is, however, a revival which promises to be permanent, and orders an reaching St. Helens from abroad, i notably Ameri ca. Thouo not the largest chemical centre n the kingdom, St. Heleilq however, has amongst its population a few thousan( chemical labourers, and to these the cheering news will b, acceptable.

div.head: TEE SALVATIONISTS.
div.p: TEE SALVATIONISTS.

Monday was a grand time for the followers of Captain Booth, who received strong reinforcements from Northwich and surrounding places. The day was commenced by a "Baptism of Fire" (?), at which there was a great amount of what these religionists describe as "knee firing," when they take what Bunyan called "the battle-axe of all prayer." After a capital tea in the Foresters' Hall, in the afternoon, a "grand hosannah meeting" was held, conducted by Captain Inman, the anti-smoker, assisted by the "Black Prince,"— we need hardly say net the one who struck such terror in the hearts of the French soldiers—" Happy Charley," "The Hallelujah Fidler," "Happy Joe," Hallelujah Scotchman," "Converted Welshman, and others.

THE SUNDAY SCHOOLS. The united demonstration of the Nonconformist Sunday schools proved very successful, considering the changeable character of the weather. The superintendents, teachers, scholars, and friends assembled at their various schoolrooms about one o'clock, and, shortly after, had a general muster, after which they were headed by the Mill Brow Sunday school brass band, and marched by way of Church-street, Regent-street, High-street, Bridge-street, and Halton-road, to a geld in the occupation of Mr. Joseph Knowles, at Halton Brook. The following was the order of procession: —Brunswick Wesleyan, St. John's Calvinistic Methodists, Bethesda Congregational. St. Luke's Mission, United Methodist Free Church, Regent-street Primitive Methodist, Mill Brow Wesleyan, Camden Wesleyan, and Nelson-street Wesleyan. The scholars of the United Methodist Free Church schools carried beautiful bouquets, composed of ferns, rhododendrons, and other flowers. About 4,000 scholars and friends took part in the procession, the mem- bers of which had, however, to disperse very soon after reaching the field, owing to a heavy fall of rain. On re- turning to the school-rooms, tea was provided, and the even- ing spent in a variety of pleasant ways. The scholars of the Parish Church schools, strengthened by those from the Newtown Mission, met about one in the afternoon, and marched through Church-street, High-street, avid Greenway-road to the Vicarage, at Higher Runcorn, and then to Runcfrn Hill, headed by their own band. After [having spent a merry time in various games, they walked back to the schoolroom and had tea. Dancing and various other amusements followed. The Holy Trinity Sunday school scholars, after walking through the town to Duke's field, and playing at certain games, had tea. The boat children under Mr. Shaw, the seamen's missionary, met at their echoolroom, Bottom Locks, and formed in procession. Wagons were provided for the younger portion, and the school attracted much attention owing to the playing of the newly formed drum and fife band, under the able leadership of Mr. W. Cooper. The "bandsmen" were attired in man- of-war's dress, and they made capital specimens of youthful British tare. Let us hope they may prove good sailors on life's spiritual voyage, and "anchor safe at last" in the harbour where there are no rude blasts to meet. On Tuesday the scholars, teachers, and friends of the Mill Brow (Runcorn) and Weston Wesleyan Methodist Sunday schools had a trip down the river to Liverpool in the steamers Fairy Queen and Rover. With the exception of a little rain, all passed off very pleasantly. On Tuesday morning an excursion under the auspices of the friends at Bethesda Congregational Chapel left the Runcorn station at half-past five for Windermere, and did not reach Runcorn on the return journey until two o'clock on the following morn- ing. The weather proved very unpropitious, and as many of the fair visitors were dressed entirely in summer clothing, they bad a very ba.l time of it. They, however, made the best of an unpleasant fix, and the more venturesome visited Bowness, Ambleside, Wordsworth's grave, and other well- known interesting points.

div.head: WIDNES.
div.p: WIDNES.

One would have thought that tho present depressed state of matters in the chemical trade would have bad a very depressing effect upon all holiday makers, but this was not found to be the case in the town of Widnes on Monday and Tuesday. Thousands lett by train for various places, in- cluding Manchester, Warrington, St. Helens, and different parts of Cheshire. On Monday, about 700 excursionists were sent off from the London and North-Western station to Blackpool, the queen of Lancashire watering places, under the auspices of the Widnes Sick and Burial Society. An excursion train also left for Belle Vile, on which were about 500 passengers. On Tuesday the Good Templars had a successful trip to Southport, about 400 people being booked. The Central line had trips to Belle Vue on Whit-Monday and Tuesday,. and they were very well patronised. The attractions usually to be found atthat much maligned place, Widnes fair, were placed near what was formerly the Snig-pie House, and appeared to find many visitors. On the river were to be seen a number of pleasure boats containing many people who, as usual, would have been safer on land, as the manner in which they handled their frail crafts, at times, showed they wero in great danger of finding a watery grave. An enormous number passed over the railway footbridge to Runcorn, nothwithstanding the fact that the weather was far from being all that could have been desired. Speaking generally, Widnes presented quite a deserted appearance on both Monday and Tuesday, as most of the principal works were entirely stopped.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

A large number of persons visited Frodsham on Monday, the atfraction being the • usual promenade of the friendly societies. The precession consisted of tl.O Foresters, Druids, and Oddfellows' each headed by a band and banner, but there were not many members walking, considering that upwards of IWO are on the books; in fact, a large number seem to take very little interest in the annual display, with its attendant expenses, and doubtful benefit to the societies. The usual service was held at the boys' school, Overton, as some objections were raised at the last moment to attending the iron church, and hasty arrangements had to be made at the boys' school, were the Bev. H. D. Havard, vicar of Helsby, officiated in the absence of the Rev. H. B. Blegg. The clubs afterwards visited the vicarage, Mrs. John Hayes, and Castle Park, the seat of Mr. E. A. Wright, J.P., the grounds of the latter ' being thrown open to the general public, the extensive

div.head: PRESCOT.
div.p: PRESCOT.

Whit-Monday, as usual, was observed at Prescot, by the closing of the principal shops and the general cessation of business. As on former occasions the inhabitants of the town took advantage of the fine weather to have a day's outing, either at the water side or further inland, and while some went to Manchester, scores visited Liverpool and thee to New Brighton, Seacombe, and Eastham, but by far the largest number proceeded to Southport, a great many accompanying the Oddfellows of the Prescot district, by the first train in the morning, About a thousand persons passed through the gates of the station. Most of the ordinary trains were well laden, and during the day two or three ex- cursion trains, full of passengers, passed through the station from the north. The omnibuses to and from Liverpool and St. Helens were also well patronised, and in the course of the day hundreds of conveyances of all descriptions, and bicy- clists passed through the town.

div.head: HUYTON.
div.p: HUYTON.

The number of passengers booked here for Liverpool was scarcely so large as on last Whit-Monday. A large number of persons alighted at the station for the Liberal demonstra- tion in Knowsley-park, and also for the plc-rile, at Roby. Several excursion trains, with their living freights, passed through the station to and from Liverpool. ROBY.

On Whit-Monday, a pic-nic to commemorate the "George Stephenson centenary," was held at the Stanley Arms Hotel, Roby, under distinguished patronage. Over 70 sat down to a capital tea provided and served up by Mr. A. C. Doe, in the ball-raom, and after tea the proceedings were enlivened by songs, die., by several of those present. During the after- noon dancing was indulged in to a large extent on the bowl- ing green, to the strains of an excellent string band, about 200 males and females taking part. The proceeds of the pic-nic were to be devoted to the funds of the Railway Ser- vant's Orphanage at Derby. The arrangements for the excursion and pic-nic were admirably carried out by a com- mittee, of which Mr. J. M. Rowlands, of Tunnel-road, Liver- pool, is the secretary.
ST. HELENS.

Whit-Monday, as usual, was regarded as a holiday in St. Helens. This being the day upon which hosts of people leave the town for a day's pleasure at some fashionable watering place, or some less salubrious district where pleasure can be obtained, the weather glass received more attention than is usually given to that important piece of household furniture; and anxious pleasure seekers specu- lated on the prospect of the weather. Early in the morning the weather was moderately fine, but a cold wind blew from the west, and about eleven o'clock there was a rumble of thunder, and a shower of rain. The weather, however, cleared up, and with the exception of a cold wind we have nothing te record that interfered with the day's pleasure. From ear y morn till noon the railway station was the scene of bustle and excitement. About 800 were booked to Black- pool, and the Oddfellows' trip to Southport carried away about 1,350, of which number 350 were booked by the com- pany. Liverpool is not without attraction to St. Helens people, and to this placed about 600 were booked. Nearly 500 were conveyed to Manchester with the object of a day's [pleasure in the garden's at Belle Vue, and a goodly number 11 were taken to Prescot ostensibly for the purpose of joining in the demonstration at Knowsley Park. In St. Helens, nearly all the shops were closed, and large numbers of people assembled in the streets to witness the procession of the various Bands of Hope in the district, this being the principal, if not the only, feature of interest in the town on Whit-Monday. Between one and two o'clock the various branches of the Union, which numbers over 4,000 members, assembled in front of the Tows Hall to form into procession. The Mayor showed his interest in the demonstration by appearing before the gathering on the Town Hall steps, and expressed himself much pleased at the sight. The spectacle certainly was a very imposing one, the children particularly being dressed with all the extra pains demanded by the occasion. The procession, leaving the Town Hall, headed by the Peasley Cross Band, proceeded through Corporation- street, Shaw-street, Raven-street, Church-street, Bridge- street, Liverpool-road, Westfield-street, Baldwin-street, Duke-street, to the cricket field at Denton's Green. At con- venient distances in the procession there were the Pemberton Bass Band, the Borough Brass Band, Messrs. Eccles and Webster's brass band, Presbyterian fife band, Eccleston fife band, and the Sutton Wesleyan Methodist fife band. Banners and bannerettes, with mottoes, adorned the procession. Arrived at the field, the members of each branch marched to their own cart, from which supplies were taken and handed to the hungry youngsters. After a short time bad elapsed the usual games commenced, and balloons, to the immense delight of the youngsters, were let off, some of which were lost in the clouds. " Kiss in the ring" attracted young men and maidens, who alike pursued the game with ardour aril zest. There were brass and fife band contests, bicycle races, singing and speaking contests announced, but the speaking contest did not come off. Ihe one-and-a-half mile bicycle race attracted considerable attention. J. Har- wood, the scratch man, reached the gaol first; E. Hulme, who bad 140 yards' start, cams in second; and W. H. Leach, who had 130 yards' start, secured the third place. Ancther race was run, in which R. M. Prescott proved the winner. The children's one-mile bicycle race was won by J. G. Stur- giess, seven years of age. The brass band contest, from which Pemberton band was excluded, resulted in the prize being awarded to the borough hand, of which Mr. Isaac Hall is cenductor. The Eccleston fife band (conductor, Mr. Geo. Parr) carried away the prize in the fife band contest. Messrs. Wright and Hayes were the judges in the lbind contests. The singing contest may be considered as a failure, as only one choir put in an appearance—the Pri- mitive Methodist, Parr Stocks, to which choir the prize was given. Three copper kettles were awarded for the three neatest, cleanest, and best turn-outs in the horses and carts. John Platt, driver of the cart with the Baptist branch, was awarded the first prize ;' James Glover, driving one of Mess, s. Pilkington's horses with Peasley Cross branch, the second; and Henry Fildes, with the United Methodist Free Church branch, the third. Extra prizes were awarded to T. Fletcher, with Park-road Wesleyan branch, and Peter Bold, with Peasley Cross branch. The number of persons on the field was between nine and ten thousand, and it is said to be the most successful field day the union has had, except the one held in Sherdley Park about nine years ago. The middle portion of the cricket field being "roped off" to pre- vent any encroachment upon the rolled ground, made it rather awkward, thereby limiting the space very perceptibly, and it was a very difficult matter to prevent the young people from running into forbidden ground. About six o'clock a shower of rain fell, causing many to leave the field, and soon afterwards the bands turned their steps homewards, and ultimately the field was cleared. The committee are to be congratulated on the success of the affair, and much praise is due to Mr. J. B. Leach, the president of the union, and to all those who assisted him, in providing a treat for the young people.

iIITRDEROI:7B ASSAULT AT BLAnCBUILtiL - Thomas Strickland, spinner, 36 years of age, is in custody at Black- burn, charged with a murderous assault upon his wife. Dur- ing a quarrel on Sunday morning, he struck her two violent blows on the head with a poker, inflicting such injuries that she now lies in a precarious condition at the infirmary. He gave himself up at night, owing to a rumour that his wife was dead. The magistrates on Tuesday remanded him for eight days. NONCOIrORIVIST MARRIAGE.—Mr. Bodes°, M.P., speak- ing at the opening of a Wesleyan bazaar at Par, on Tuesday, said ot the bills before the House of Commons affecting non- conformists there was one to which he wished to call their attention, because his name was on the back of it. It was a bill brought in by his friend Mr. Briggs, and its object was that at nonconformist marriages the registrar should no longer be required. There was this difficulty—they must find somebody to take the responsibility the registrar now discharged. Mr. Borlase would not ask the ministers to take that responsibility, however willing they might be. He did not think the ministers should take upon themselves any state responsibility whatever. He thought the contracting parties were sufficiently educated in these days to take the duty upon themselves, and to transmit to the registrar the certifiaate which the minister would draw up and sign for them.

div.head: BRUTAL MURDER AT PRESCOT.
div.p: BRUTAL MURDER AT PRESCOT.

KICKING A WIFE TO DEATH. On Saturday right last, a most brutal and aggravated murder was perpetrated at Prescot, the victim being a mar- ried woman named Margaret Fitzpatrick. Shortly after ten o'clock a young Irish labourer named James Fitzpatrick, a man well known to the police, residing in Brown's-square, Eccleston-street, Prescot, while in an intoxicated condition quarrelled with his wife. Hard words passed, and eventu- ally the woman left the house, followed by the prisoner, who overtook her and struck her violently with a short poker, whidi he carried in his hand, and knocked her down. While upon the ground the prisoner kicked his wife two or three times on various parts of the body, he wearing at the time a pair of heavily soled militia boots, which were studded with " star " nails. The fellow then got hold of the unfortunate woman by the hair of the head and dragged her towards the door of her house, and when she was in the act of rising to her feet he again kicked her most brutally and unmercifully about the abdomen, inflicting serious wounds and causieg blood to flow freely. The poor woman was carried into the house, and P.S. Bell was called in. On arrival he perceived that the woman was in a dying state, and he at once went for Dr. Hall, but before the latter arrived upon the scene she had succumbed to the injuries she had received, after about, half an hour's intense suffer- ing. The floor of the house was literally covered with blood, and almost everything in the house was in com- plete disorder. On hearing that the woman was dead, P.S. Bull immediately took the prisoner into custody and charged him with having murdered his wife. Prisoner replied "Not me; I've done nothing; I've not caused her death." He was then taken to the police station and locked up. On Sunday a post mortens ex- amination of the body was made by Dr. Hall, and on Mon- day the prisoner was brought before Mr. W. L. Evans at the Prescot Police Court, and remanded till Tuesday next. The affair has created much excitement and consternation amongst the inhabitants of the town, and loud were the complaints against the prisoner for the brutal and cruel manner in which he had treated his wife. Although there have been many cases of unlawfully wounding in the town, it is some fifty years since the last murder occurred, when a wife cut her husband's throat with a razor. THE INQUEST. The inquest on the body of the murdered woman was held at the Court-house, Derby-street, on Tuesday, by Mr. F. Smith, coroner for the manor of Prescot, and a jury of which Mr. Thomas Prescott, of Stanley Cresent, was the foreman. There were also present Mr. Blackwell (assistant magistrates' clerk), and Mr. Inspector Barnett, and the prisoner. During the hearing of the evidence, the street in the neighbourhood of the court, was crowded with people, eager to learn the result of the inquiry; and when the verdict was made known, they gave vent to their feelings by exclaiming "Serves him right; he deserves to be hung." The crowd soon afterwards dispersed. The Coroner, in opening the proceedings, said the cause of their meeting that day was a very solemn and serious one. It was to ascertain the cause of death of a woman and then by whom that cause of death arose. He thought the evidence which would be produced before them would en- tirely satisfy them on all points, and he hoped it would not be necessary, as at first they thought it would be, to adjourn the inquiry to a future occasion. Ellen Black, widow, residing at Tea-street, Prescot, said: Deceased was mv daughter, and was 28 years of age. She had been married to the prisoner between seven and eight years, and had had five children. While standing at my house door on Saturday night I heard a noise in Brown's- square and went thither to ascertain the cause. When I got there I saw the prisoner striking his wife, who was on the ground, on the back and arms with a poker. At that time they were at their own door. I took off one of my boots and hit the prisoner in the face with it, and he im- mediately struck me a blow on the knee with the poker. I then got held of the deceased to lift her up, but the pri- soner kicked her and knocked her down again. Prisoner then got hold of deceased by the hair of the head and dragged her towards the door of the house. Deceased cried out "Oh, mother, dear, I am killed." My daughter Ann then came up and endeavoured to take me away, and 49 I was going I saw the prisoner again kick the deceased twice. I then went away and did not see her alive again. The Foreman (Mr. Prescott): In what state was the pri- soner? Was he drunk? Witness: He had had drink, but was not drunk. Mr. Taylor: Were you sober? Witness: Yes. Dr. Hall: You had had drink when I saw you, had you not Witness: No, I had not.—Dr. Hall: You seemed as if you had had drink. By Inspector. Barnett: The poker produced is the one the prisoner struck the deceased with. He had hold of it by the thick end. The boots produced are similar to those the pri- soner had on at the time. Prisoner had thrashed deceased many times. I have heard the prisoner say many times, when intoxicated, that he would kill his wife. On one oc- casion he threw a stool at her, which hit her on the head, and inflicted a wound. Prisoner was once locked up for 14 days for ill-using his wife. When I saw deceased, on the morning of last Saturday, she was in good health. Ann Black, residing with her mother at Tea-st., Prescot, said: Deceased was my sister. Between ten and half-past ten o'clock on Saturday night I was in aneighbouring house when Mrs. Doyle called and told me my mother had gone towards Brown's-square. I followed her, and saw the pri- soner in the square with a poker in his hand, with which he struck the deceased. He had hold of the thin end of the poker at the hoc. I s'w my mother tato off her shoe and strike the prisoner on the back with it, and he then hit my mother a blow on the leg with the poker, and afterwards hit me twice on the back with the same instrument. I then took my mother away, and when we had proceeded A short distance we stopped, and I saw the prisoner take a running kick at the deceased, striking her in the lower portion of the body. Prisoner then took deceased by the hair of the head and dragged her towards the door, and struck her on the arm with the poker. I then went home, but returned again in about five minutes, and listened at the door of the pri- soner's house. I heard my sister moaning, and I heard her say, " Oh, I'm done." I then went to look for a policeman, and seeing Sergeant Bull coming along the Market-place I stopped and told him what had happened, and he told me to fetch two policemen, who were at the bottom of Market- place. I did so, and went up with them to Brown's-square. Sergeant Bull had gone on -before us. On arriving at the house I saw the deceased lying on a bed on the floor in a pool of blood. Deceased spoke to me and said, "Lord, have mercy on me ! I'm done. Oh, my heart." I stayed until the doctor came' and I then left. I have heard prisoner threaten to kill deceased on many occasions, and have re- peatedly seen him kicking her. I saw deceased about half- nest seven o'clock on Saturday night at my mother's house. Deceased was not intoxicated at the time; she did not take drink. I have never seen her the worse for liquor. My mother was sober that night. In answer to Mr. Garrett, witness said the prisoner was intoxicated at the time, but not drunk. Mr. Taylor: Did you say anything to make the prisoner strike you ?—Witness: Ne, I did not. By the Coroner: Beyond my mother striking the prisoner. neither I, my mother, nor the deceased did anything to aggravate him. Mr. Taylor: Were there any other persons present at the time ?—Witness : Yes ; there were plenty of persons present, but no one dare go near the prisoner while he had the poker in his hand. Mr. Taylor: Were you in any part of the prisoner's house before the row commenced ?—Witness: No, I was not. By Inspector Barnett: I am confident the shoes produced are the same the prisoner was wearing when he kicked the deceased. When I went into the house with the police the prisoner was sitting on a chair. I told prisoner that he had murdered my sister, and he said be had not done it. I then said, "How came she in this state," but prisoner did not answer. William Henry Moxey, shoemaker, residing in Daniel's- yard, off Brown's-square, said: On Saturday night last about a quarter past ten o'clock, while standing at the door of my house, I heard some women shouting, but I could not tell what they were saying. I went to Brown's-square, and saw the mother and deceased standing in the square. I saw the shutter pulled down, and the windows broken, but I could not say who broke them, as it was dark at the time. Deceased's mother endeavoured to prevent them being broken. I believe deceased and her sister broke the window. I saw James Fitzpatrick come out of his house with a poker in his hand. The poker produced is similar to the one I saw in his possession. I saw him rush at his wife and strike her several blows with it on the body. The first blow knocked her down, and the prisoner struck her while she was on the ground. Deceased got up, and the prisoner then seized her by the hair of the head and dragged her to the doorstep. At this time deceased was upon her knees, and I saw her get hold of and cling to his legs. Shortly after de- ceased left loose of his legs, and she fell backwards, and the prisoner then kicked her three or four times in the lower portion of the body. Prisoner then went into his house, and the deceased managed to crawl into the square, and I heard her say to my wife, "Go and fetch a policeman; he has kicked me in the abdomen." I then went away, and took Inv wife with me. Mr. Dennett : Hew far were you away when this affair was taking place? Witness : I was about three yards away. By the Coroner : The prisoner was intoxicated, but deceased seemed quite saber. Dr. E. F. Hall, practising in Prescot, said : On Saturday evening between twenty minutes and half-past eleven o'clock, Sergeant Bull asked me to go to Brown's-square. I accompanied him to the house, and found the deceased lying on her side on a small bed on the floor. I could hardly get near her for blood, which seemed to have saturated everything around her. I examined her and found she was _ dead. Deceased was then stripped, and I examined her and found several bruises about the left shoulder, and day injuries to other parts of the body. The House contains convenient cellaring, and on the ground floor three large and superior entertaining rooms, two roomy kitchens, pantry, and butler's pantry, and front and beck staircases, etc. On the first floor five excellent roomy bedrooms, bathroom, water-closet, with fire-place, and box room; and on the upper storey two other pleasant roomy bedrooms, with fire-places, closets, etc. There is a good supply of spring and rain water. The Offices comprise capital stabling for five horses, hay lofts, ben houses, shippon, piggeries, two roomy carriage houses and coachman's house, small greenhouse, summer house, etc. The premises are situated convenient to the Rainhill Railway Station, and the land is adaptable for separation and erection of another residence, if desired. The whole premises are in excellent order, as recently occupied by the late owner up to his death, and now by his representatives. LOT 2.—A1l that FREEHOLD FARM, situate at Hough Green, Ditton, consisting of five closes of land, crofts, orchard, farmhouse, barn, shippon, stable, and outbuildings, containing by admeasurement, about 14 acres, now in the occupation of Mr. James Haigh, or his under-tenant, as yearly tenant. This property is situate within ten minutes' walk of the Hough Green Railway Station, between Liverpool and Warrington, In a pleasant open district, The Farm is compact to the house, and the land of a nature highly suitable for market-garden culture. LOT 3.—A1l those Two FREEHOLD HOUSES or small SHOPS, situated and being Nos. 190 and 192 ia Westfield' street, St. Helens, occupied by Patrick Murphy and Mrs. Makinson, together with the unoccupied Cottages or Outbuild- ings at the back, which may be used for warehouse or business purposes. LOT 4.—A1l those Two Stone-built DWELLING-HOUSES or Cottages, freehold, situated near the Red Cat," Rainford, to- gether with the gardens, back and front, and outbuildings and appurtenances belonging thereto, in the occupation of Mrs. Pennington and another. LOT 5.—A1l those Four FREEHOLD COTTAGES, with the vacant land and appurtenances belonging thereto, now occu- pied as two tenements, situate and being at Alma Hill, in Up- holland, in the said county, now in the occupations of Sarah Aspinall and William Gaskell, as tenants; and also the Three Freehold Cottages almost adjoining to the above, with the land and appurtenances thereto, situate to the front of the said Alma Hill, now in the occupations of Sarah Aspinall, senior, Richard Green, and another, as tenants. LOT B.—All those Three FREEHOLD COTTAGES. situate at Stair Brow, or Back Brow, in Upholland aforesaid, with the land and appurtenances thereto. Intending purchasers of Lot 1 will be admitted to view the same, on application at the premises; and the respective tenants of the other premises will show the properties; and further particulars may be obtained, as to the Upholland Cot- tages, on application to Mr. ABRAHAM BETLEY, at Upholland; and as to all the lots, to ALEXANDER CROSS, Esq., Rainhill ; or Messrs. BARROW & COOK, Solicitors, St. Helens.
